articleBody:
BERLIN. **Verdreckte Toiletten, fehlende Privatsphäre, unangenehme Gerüche: Was für viele Schülerinnen und Schüler zum Alltag gehört, hat Folgen, die weit über den Zustand der sanitären Anlagen hinausgehen. Manche Kinder und Jugendliche vermeiden es sogar, während des Schultags zu trinken, um nicht auf die Toilette gehen zu müssen. Dabei können Schulen durchaus etwas verändern – und die Betroffenen selbst spielen dabei eine entscheidende Rolle. Wie das gelingen kann, zeigt eine kostenlose Online-Veranstaltung der Heinz Trox-Stiftung am 25. November, die News4teachers als Medienpartner unterstützt.**

Die Toilette gehört zu den wenigen Orten in einer Schule, an denen Schülerinnen und Schüler für einen Moment unbeobachtet sein können. Eigentlich. Denn vielerorts sind die sanitären Anlagen in einem Zustand, der Kinder und Jugendliche eher abschreckt, als ihnen einen geschützten Raum zu bieten. Verschmutzungen, beschädigte Einrichtungen und fehlende Rückzugsmöglichkeiten können dazu führen, dass Schülerinnen und Schüler den Toilettengang möglichst lange hinauszögern.

Wie weitreichend die Folgen sein können, verdeutlicht eine Untersuchung der German Toilet Organization (GTO) und der Universität Bonn, deren Ergebnisse 2023 veröffentlicht wurden. Befragt wurden 949 Neuntklässlerinnen und Neuntklässler an 17 weiterführenden Schulen in Berlin. Sie bewerteten ihre Schultoiletten durchschnittlich mit der Schulnote 4 minus. 46 Prozent gaben an, das Wasserlassen in der Schule zu vermeiden, beim Stuhlgang waren es sogar 85 Prozent. Mehr als ein Viertel der Befragten berichtete, deshalb oft oder immer weniger zu essen oder zu trinken.

Damit wird aus einem vermeintlichen Problem der Gebäudeunterhaltung eine Frage der Gesundheit und des Wohlbefindens. Doch wer kann daran etwas ändern? Und wie lassen sich Schülerinnen und Schüler an Verbesserungen beteiligen, statt lediglich neue Verhaltensregeln für die Toilettennutzung aufzustellen?

Diesen Fragen widmet sich die zweite Ausgabe des digitalen Gesprächsformats „ZUKUNFTSRAUM SCHULE LIVE“ der Heinz Trox-Stiftung. Unter dem Titel „Raus aus der Schmuddelecke: Schultoiletten als erweiterter Lehrraum“ diskutieren am Mittwoch, 25. November 2026, von 16 bis 17 Uhr Thilo Panzerbieter, Gründer und Geschäftsführer der German Toilet Organization, und Lilian Ruß, Leiterin der Initiative „Toiletten machen Schule“.

## „Schüler*innen kennen ihre Schultoiletten meist am besten. Sie nutzen sie jeden Tag, haben aber selten etwas mit Ausstattung und Instandhaltung zu tun“

Im Mittelpunkt steht ein Ansatz, der über die Sanierung beschädigter Toiletten hinausgeht: Schülerinnen und Schüler sollen selbst daran mitwirken, die Situation zu erfassen, Probleme zu benennen und Lösungen zu entwickeln. Aus einem Ort, der im Schulalltag häufig Anlass für Beschwerden ist, kann so ein Raum werden, in dem Beteiligung und Verantwortung praktisch erfahrbar werden.

„Schüler*innen kennen ihre Schultoiletten meist am besten. Sie nutzen sie jeden Tag, haben aber selten etwas mit Ausstattung und Instandhaltung zu tun. Wenn wir ihre Perspektive einbeziehen und sie selbst entscheiden, was mit diesem Raum passiert und wie er aussieht, wächst auch ihr Verantwortungsbewusstsein. Und sie erfahren an diesem stillen Ort ganz konkret, was Teilhabe und Selbstwirksamkeit bedeuten“, sagt Lilian Ruß.

Die Initiative „Toiletten machen Schule“ unterstützt Schulen dabei, einen solchen Prozess selbst zu organisieren. Ein kostenfreies Hilfsportal stellt dafür Umfragetools, Checklisten, Beteiligungsmethoden und Praxisbeispiele bereit. Schulen können zunächst ein Toilettenteam gründen, anschließend gemeinsam mit den Schülerinnen und Schülern den Zustand der Anlagen untersuchen und schließlich Maßnahmen entwickeln und priorisieren.

Dabei geht es nicht allein um die Gestaltung der Räume. Auch Fragen der Reinigung, der Instandhaltung und des Umgangs miteinander müssen geklärt werden. Für nachhaltige Verbesserungen ist deshalb die Zusammenarbeit verschiedener Beteiligter wichtig: Schülerinnen und Schüler, Lehrkräfte, Schulleitungen, Eltern, Hausmeisterei, Reinigungspersonal und Schulträger müssen gemeinsam Lösungen finden.

Allerdings können Schulen nicht sämtliche Probleme in Eigenregie beheben. Die regelmäßige Reinigung, die Instandhaltung der Anlagen und die Beseitigung baulicher Schäden liegen wesentlich in der Verantwortung der zuständigen Schulträger und Dienstleister. Beteiligungsprojekte können dazu beitragen, Missstände sichtbar zu machen, Prioritäten zu setzen und den Umgang mit den Räumen zu verändern. Sie ersetzen aber nicht die notwendigen Investitionen und organisatorischen Maßnahmen.

Für die Heinz Trox-Stiftung ist die Beschäftigung mit Schultoiletten Teil einer umfassenderen Frage: Welche räumlichen Bedingungen brauchen Kinder und Jugendliche, um sich in der Schule wohlzufühlen und gut lernen zu können?

Mit ihrem Projekt „Zukunftsraum Schule“ beschäftigt sich die Stiftung insbesondere mit Temperatur, Akustik, Innenraumluft und Licht. Diese vier Faktoren werden im sogenannten TAIL-Ansatz gemeinsam betrachtet. Die Qualität schulischer Räume soll dabei nicht nur anhand einzelner technischer Merkmale bewertet werden, sondern in ihrem Zusammenspiel.

Auch die Schultoiletten gehören aus Sicht der Stiftung zu einer solchen Betrachtung. Schließlich verbringen Schülerinnen und Schüler ihren Tag nicht ausschließlich im Klassenzimmer. Flure, Aufenthaltsbereiche, Pausenräume und sanitäre Anlagen prägen ebenfalls ihre Erfahrungen mit Schule.

„Mit Zukunftsraum Schule setzen wir uns für Räume ein, in denen Kinder gut lernen und sich wohlfühlen können. Das endet nicht an der Klassenzimmertür. Wer über Luft, Licht, Temperatur und Akustik spricht, muss auch die Orte mitdenken, die Kinder jeden Tag nutzen und oft meiden. Die Schultoilette zeigt zudem, wie viel sich bewegt, wenn Schüler*innen ihre Räume selbst bewerten und mitgestalten“, erklärt Christine Roßkothen, Vorstand der Heinz Trox-Stiftung.

Im Online-Gespräch soll deshalb auch zur Sprache kommen, welche Bedeutung beispielsweise Lüftung, Beleuchtung und Temperatur für sanitäre Anlagen haben und was sich aus den Beteiligungsverfahren der Initiative für andere Bereiche der Schule lernen lässt.

Die Veranstaltung richtet sich an Lehrkräfte, Schulleitungen, Schülerinnen und Schüler, Eltern, Schulträger sowie Verantwortliche aus Schulverwaltung, Planung und Bildungspolitik. Nach den Impulsen der beiden Gäste ist ein offener Austausch mit den Teilnehmenden vorgesehen. *News4teachers*

**Die Teilnahme an „ZUKUNFTSRAUM SCHULE LIVE“ ist kostenlos.** **Die Veranstaltung findet am Mittwoch, 25. November 2026, von 16 bis 17 Uhr online über Zoom statt. Eine Anmeldung ist über die [Anmeldeseite der Veranstaltung](https://events.zoom.us/ev/AuJ19hdL1mRjVOlhBZP-5j5cEhmui60vz1EcQzwHVOKCQdhYECaN~Asob29Q2tmMxwekwG6sOFngO719v87MLZss9STDzltI03xasY4AVz7QwrA?utm_source=chatgpt.com) möglich.**

Weitere Informationen und Materialien finden Interessierte auf den Internetseiten von [Toiletten machen Schule](https://toiletten-machen-schule.de/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) und [Zukunftsraum Schule LIVE](https://www.zukunftsraum-schule.de/projekte-dialog/zukunftsraum-schule-live/?utm_source=chatgpt.com). News4teachers unterstützt die Veranstaltung als Medienpartner.

## Why you should be reading Helen Garner (and where to start).

Last week, The Paris Review announced the winners of its annual literary awards. In 2027, Australian author Helen Garner will be feted with the Hadada, a prize that recognizes a writer’s lifelong literary contributions. I am here as an independent body to hype this choice.

Garner—a novelist, journalist, and diarist—writes big-hearted heroines who are often on the edge of a crisis. Her other fans include Lauren Groff, Lily King, Rumaan Alam, and Ben Lerner, but we are legion. Why, you ask?

In a recent piece for The Guardian , Emma Brockes also praised Garner’s “ability to combine insight and erudition of the highest literary order with a style that is at times comically down to earth.” And it’s true—that earthiness is what makes her work indelible. But it’s also just the tip of an iceberg.

Here are three of Garner’s best known books (and why you should make like the Parisians and pick them up, stat).

Monkey Grip , Garner’s 1977 debut, sent a shockwave through Australia. This novel chronicles a woman’s doomed-from-the-jump situationship with a heroin addict who charms her intermittently as they orbit a communal living situation.

A little like Susie Boyt’s sleeper hit, Loved and Missed , this book beautifully captures the recurring heartbreak involved in loving an addict. But it’s never saccharine, or sanctimonious.

Following a bohemian Melbourne milieu that echoes the author’s own set at the time, Garner’s non-judgmental portrait of freewheeling radicals brought out the moralizers on publication. Nora, our heroine, ruffled feathers for depicting ambivalent parenthood administered with a very loose latchkey. All adults in this book are libidinally motivated. Drugs and sex are world-structuring forces.

But what’s most exciting is how naked the prose is about all of that want. In Garner’s matter-of-fact voice, Nora’s thirst for the grifting Javo is rendered tender, abject, holy, and pathetic by turns. She feels like a real and vulnerable person with a mighty human flaw. The best kind of protagonist.

My favorite of Garner’s novels is The Children’s Bach . Another tale of domestic upheaval ignited by a charismatic chaos agent, this book traces the happily partnered Athena Fox’s infatuation with a blast from the past. Against reason, she leaves her partner and two small children for… a rock star.

What follows is a little predictable, but as with Monkey Grip the pleasure is in experiencing that slow road to ruin. (Or is it ecstasy?)

The third person POV serves this book, which manages to texturize everyone affected by Athena’s choices. She feels like a modern Nora, in the Ibsen sense.

The Spare Room is a cool, slim, spiky book. I find this Garner still gnaws at me. Following two semi-estranged old friends who fall back together when one seeks harbor following a terminal diagnosis, this novel depicts the unpleasant side of caretaking and the indignity of illness.

This book asks some truly itchy questions. Such as, what do you do when your patient is delusional—and/or, you want them out of your house?

As in the other novels, our protagonist chafes against conventionality and obligatory mutual obligation. And her extreme honesty hits you like a glass of cold water. As always, there’s a nakedness to a Garner subject. She doesn’t flinch from depicting those ugly emotions or unwanted thoughts.

In a review for the Times , Daphne Merkin once compared Garner to other “laconic and wayward,” ladies who specialize in the “art of artlessness, like Jean Rhys, Jane Bowles and Paula Fox.”

I agree with wayward, but I think that artful eye is in a class all its own. Do yourself a favor and join the Helen hive. Today.

### Brittany Allen

Brittany K. Allen is a writer and actor living in Brooklyn.

articleBody:
Wissenschaftskommunikation ist politischer geworden und muss sich in einer zunehmend polarisierten Welt behaupten. Annette Leßmöllmann und Markus Weißkopf sprechen zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de über Erfolge, Herausforderungen und notwendigen Wandel.

Am 24. November 2016 ging Wissenschaftskommunikation.de online. In unserem [Schwerpunkt zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wo-steht-die-wisskomm/)blicken wir auf prägende Entwicklungen zurück *und fragen, wo die Wissenschaftskommunikation heute steht.*

**Mit welcher Idee und welchem persönlichen Anspruch seid Ihr 2016 an der Gründung von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de beteiligt gewesen?**

**Markus Weißkopf** ist Redakteur des Research.Table bei Table.Media. Er war Geschäftsführer von Wissenschaft im Dialog und hat dort unter anderem die Plattform Wissenschaftskommunikation.de aufgebaut. Foto: WiD

Markus Weißkopf: Kurz zuvor hatten Wissenschaft im Dialog und der Bundesverband Hochschulkommunikation gemeinsam die [Leitlinien zur guten Wissenschaftskommunikation](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/leitlinien-zur-guten-wissenschaftskommunikation-85129/) veröffentlicht. In dem Zuge hatte die Community viel über gemeinsame Werte, aber auch über die Professionalisierung der Wissenschaftskommunikation diskutiert. Wissenschaftskommunikation.de sollte unter anderem eine Plattform für diese Themen bieten.

Annette Leßmöllmann: Die Plattform sollte zeigen: Wissenschaftskommunikation bedeutet mehr als nur Pressemitteilungen und Hochglanzmagazine. Mir war es ein Anliegen, Forschung und Praxis zusammenzubringen und somit die [Vermittlung der Wissenschaftskommunikationsforschung](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/kategorie/forschung/) voranzutreiben. Zum einen, um praxisrelevante Ergebnisse bekannt zu machen, zum anderen, um die theoretische Weiterentwicklung, die Interdisziplinarität und die Selbstreflexion des Forschungsfeldes zu zeigen. Gleichzeitig sollten Praxisfragen für die Forschung nachvollziehbar werden, um neue Forschung anzustoßen.

**Annette Leßmöllmann** (@annetteless.bsky.social) ist promovierte Linguistin und hat am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT)* den Lehrstuhl für Wissenschaftskommunikation mit dem Schwerpunkt Linguistik inne. Sie lehrt in den Bachelor- und Master-Studiengängen „Wissenschaft – Medien – Kommunikation“ (@WMKstudium).

**Welche Fragen oder Konfliktlinien aus der Gründungszeit beschäftigen die Community bis heute?**

Weißkopf: „Als Anlaufstelle Nr. 1 hat sich das Online-Lexikon Wikipedia im Internet längst etabliert. Die Wissenschaft sollte das Potenzial von Wikipedia für die Vermittlung fundierten Wissens ernsthaft prüfen.“ Das hat eine Pressesprecherin [im Rahmen des ersten Schwerpunkts „Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation“](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/blick-nach-vorn-wie-sieht-die-wissenschaftskommunikation-der-zukunft-aus-5-13517/) geschrieben. Natürlich ist das Prüfen wissenschaftsimmanent. Aber im Bereich der Kommunikation können wir es uns nicht erlauben, jahrelang zu prüfen. Die Wissenschaft hat nun ein Engagement bei oder für [Wikipedia](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/format/wikipedia/) so lange geprüft, bis es zu spät war. Nur einzelne Einrichtungen wie die Universität Innsbruck bilden hier Ausnahmen. Da würde ich mir manchmal mehr Mut zum Experimentieren wünschen!

Leßmöllmann: Was sich bereits vor zehn Jahren angekündigt hat: Wissenschaftskommunikation muss sich für Wissenschaftsfreiheit einsetzen und ist – teilweise notgedrungen – wesentlich politischer geworden. Dass sie in Interessenslagen und Machtstrukturen eingebettet ist und dass es als machtvoller kommunikativer Akt angesehen wird, wenn jemand „bestimmt“, was wahr oder falsch ist – das war damals eher ein Gedankenexperiment, ist heute aber deutlich als Konflikt zu spüren.

Es wird für die Wissenschaftskommunikation viel schwieriger, wenn es den Entscheider*innen reicht, dass sich etwas wahr anfühlt, auch wenn es nicht wahr ist. Dass etwa politische und gesellschaftliche Entscheidungen gegen den vorherrschenden wissenschaftlichen Konsens getroffen werden, ist angesichts der Klimakrise deutlich bedrohlicher und krisenhafter spürbar als noch vor zehn Jahren.

### „Wissenschaftskommunikation muss sich für Wissenschaftsfreiheit einsetzen und ist – teilweise notgedrungen – wesentlich politischer geworden.“

Annette Leßmöllmann

**Direkt mit dem ersten Schwerpunkt des Portals haben wir damals auf die** **[Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/zukunft-der-wissenschaftskommunikation/)** **geblickt. Welche damaligen Hoffnungen und Befürchtungen haben sich aus Eurer Sicht bewahrheitet und welche nicht?**

Leßmöllmann: Es hat sich die Hoffnung bewahrheitet, dass heute stärker darauf geachtet wird, Kommunikationsaktivitäten wissenschaftlich fundiert zu evaluieren. Zudem hat es funktioniert, dass sich die Community intensiver vernetzt und dass Forschung und Praxis enger zusammenarbeiten.

Es gab auch den Wunsch, dass Wissenschaftskommunikation stärker Teil der Gesellschaft und des täglichen Austauschs über die relevanten Themen der Zeit wird. In einem Aspekt hat sich der Wunsch bewahrheitet, allerdings anders als gedacht: Durch [generative Künstliche Intelligenz](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/themen/kuenstliche-intelligenz/) sind Wissen und Wissenschaft jetzt noch einfacher und dialogischer zu erreichen.

Gleichzeitig wurde die DIN-Norm der Kommunikation aufgeweicht: Es ist nicht mehr sicher, ob das Kommunizierte auch stimmt. Dies trägt zu einer Wissenskrise bei. Etwas dystopisch und pointiert formuliert: Gesagt und geglaubt wird, was gut klingt und auf die Interessen der eigenen Peer Group einzahlt. Das zeigt, dass wir in einer völlig anderen Welt als vor zehn Jahren leben. Die Rolle des Wissens, die demokratische Verankerung und die Wissenschaftsfreiheit stehen zur Debatte.

Das Gründungs-Team (ohne Markus Weißkopf) bei der Präsentation der Plattform im Dezember 2016. Thorsten Witt, Esther Kähler, Beatrice Lugger, Annette Leßmöllmann, Christian Humm und Ulrike Brandt-Bohne. Foto: Gesine Born/WiD.

**Was muss gute Wissenschaftskommunikation heute leisten, was bei der Gründung des Portals noch eine deutlich geringere Rolle gespielt hat?**

Weißkopf: Natürlich markierten der Brexit und die Wahl Trumps im Jahr 2016 nochmal eine Beschleunigung des Populismus, doch einige Entwicklungen waren schon abzusehen. Dennoch muss man sagen, dass die Macht der Tech-Konzerne, die autokratischen Tendenzen auch im „alten Westen“ und der Aufstieg der Rechten aus der Perspektive von 2016 ein Worst Case-Szenario darstellen. Dazu kommen der Ukraine-Krieg und die Konflikte im Nahen Osten.

Mit diesem veränderten geopolitischen und Kommunikationsumfeld muss die Wissenschaftskommunikation umgehen: Kann ich noch guten Gewissens auf X sein? Wie spreche ich über China-Kooperationen meiner Einrichtungen? Muss sich meine Einrichtung politisch positionieren? Die [Debatte über ein Verbot von Zivilklauseln](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wer-erklaert-die-bedrohung-sicherheit-als-neue-aufgabe-der-wissenschaftskommunikation-100967/) zeigt exemplarisch, wie sich hier die Diskurse verändert haben.

### „Die Debatte über ein Verbot von Zivilklauseln zeigt exemplarisch, wie sich hier die Diskurse verändert haben.“

Markus Weißkopf

Leßmöllmann: Wenn man an Themen wie [Militär- oder Verteidigungsforschung](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/schwerpunkt-sicherheit-innovation/) denkt, die aus Sicherheitsgründen nicht immer öffentlich verhandelt werden können, dürfen oder sollen, wird deutlich, dass die Wissenschaftskommunikation vor Herausforderungen steht, was zum Beispiel Forderungen nach Transparenz und Dialog betrifft.

Auch wird heute deutlicher als noch vor zehn Jahren: Die Geistes- und Sozialwissenschaften sind immens wichtig, da sie Phänomene wie Migration, Demokratieabbau und Polarisierung beschreiben oder sogar erklären können. Heutzutage reicht es jedoch nicht mehr aus, sie sichtbarer zu machen. Man muss sie auch schützen, da sie teilweise mit unerträglichem Hass konfrontiert sind.

**Wo sollten Wissenschaftskommunikation.de und die Wissenschaftskommunikation insgesamt im Jahr 2036 stehen?**

Weißkopf: Wir haben nicht bis zum Jahr 2036 Zeit, um etwas zu ändern. Es geht jetzt darum, wirkungsvolle Wissenschaftskommunikation im Sinne der Leitlinien zu betreiben. Das bedeutet auch, dass man für gemeinsame Ziele den Konkurrenzgedanken beiseitelegen und Kooperationen anstreben sollte. Dafür braucht es Ressourcen für gemeinnützige Kommunikation. Diese können nur von den Leitungen bereitgestellt werden, müssen aber auch von den Kommunikator*innen eingefordert werden.

Leßmöllmann: Ich wünsche mir, dass das Portal als Stimme der Professionalität und des Austauschs zwischen Theorie und Praxis erhalten bleibt – und auch als Anlaufpunkt und Anker in schwierigen Zeiten. Wir betreiben unabhängigen Fachjournalismus und werden international dafür beneidet.

### „Ich wünsche mir, dass das Portal als Stimme der Professionalität und des Austauschs zwischen Theorie und Praxis erhalten bleibt – und auch als Anlaufpunkt und Anker in schwierigen Zeiten.“

Annette Leßmöllmann

Das Portal würde im Jahr 2036 anders aussehen, aber der Spirit wäre derselbe. Wir denken und schreiben selbst (siehe unsere [Policy zur KI-Nutzung](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/netiquette/)) und übernehmen die Verantwortung dafür, dass wir die Forschungs- und Praxislandschaft qualifiziert beobachten und sowohl aktuell als auch hintergründig darauf reagieren. Und wir geben Praktiker*innen und Forscher*innen eine Plattform.

**Gibt es einen Beitrag, Schwerpunkt oder Moment aus zehn Jahren Wissenschaftskommunikation.de, der Euch besonders in Erinnerung geblieben ist?**

Weißkopf: Es ist schwierig einen einzelnen Beitrag herauszuheben. Grundsätzlich finde ich es großartig, dass es gelungen ist, einen Ort für die Information über die Forschung zur Wissenschaftskommunikation zu schaffen. Das war mir, war uns, ein sehr wichtiges Anliegen: Die Evidenz aus der Forschung zu nutzen! Es kann nicht sein, dass ausgerechnet die Wissenschaftskommunikation sich nicht an den Erkenntnissen aus der Wissenschaft orientiert. Aber gerade das war in einem noch jungen Berufsfeld und ebenfalls recht jungen Forschungsfeld eine Herausforderung. Dass diese Forschung nun sichtbarer ist, ist sicher ein Verdienst von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de.

[Wo steht die Wisskomm? Alle Beiträge zum Schwerpunkt](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wo-steht-die-wisskomm/)

Leßmöllmann: Jedes Mal, wenn nach Monaten des Planens, Antragschreibens und Zitterns die Bewilligungsschreiben für die Weiterfinanzierung der Plattform kamen, haben Herausgeber*innen und Redaktion sehr gefeiert. Das waren besondere Momente: Nicht nur weitermachen zu können, sondern auch neue Ideen umzusetzen. Ein ganz besonderer Moment dauerte sogar eine ganze Woche: Der Designsprint mit der Deutschen Journalistenschule 2025, bei dem sich toller journalistische Nachwuchs in unser Portal reingekniet hat. Daraus ist unser großartiger [LinkedIn-Kanal](https://www.linkedin.com/company/wissenschaftskommunikation-de/) entstanden.
body: Annette Leßmöllmann und Markus Weißkopf sprechen zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de über Erfolge, Herausforderungen und notwendigen Wandel. Am 24. November 2016 ging Wissenschaftskommunikation.de online. In unserem Schwerpunkt zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum blicken wir auf prägende Entwicklungen zurück und fragen, wo die Wissenschaftskommunikation heute steht. Mit welcher Idee und welchem persönlichen Anspruch seid Ihr 2016 an der Gründung von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de beteiligt gewesen?…

## Bickering Buildings A Dialogue Between the Churches of Athens in 1854

The churches of Athens had much to say in 1854, when an anonymous author staged a squabble between them in newsprint. Nikos Magouliotis eavesdrops on this chatter, finding personified anxieties about Greek architectural identity, foreign influence, and the newly formed nation’s relation to its past.

Published

November 24, 2026

Gabriel de Rumine’s 1858 photograph of Athens from the Acropolis. The Metropolitan Cathedral is under construction in the foreground — Source .

Buildings are often thought of as “silent witnesses of history”, but they have a history of talking, especially in moments of crisis. In a pamphlet published in London in 1641, at the height of the Reformation, two monuments that served as sites of Catholic devotion literally converse, trying to make sense of (and poke fun at) the Protestant vandalism against them. 1 In the eighteenth century, a whole genre of texts developed in which authors imagined what buildings might have said if they could speak to each other or passersby. 2

This was not just a matter for the popular press. The end of the eighteenth century saw the emergence of “architecture parlante” (speaking architecture), through a group of architects who argued that buildings ought to communicate their function and meaning to people, through figurative symbols, letters, or inscriptions. 3 When opinions about a certain monument or a cityscape predominate, buildings must speak for themselves to set things straight. This happened through experimental designs by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux and others, but also through pamphlets, broadsheets, cartoons, and newspaper articles that were written for a broader public and gave voice to the built environment. 4

In mid-nineteenth-century Athens, the furious construction of the new capital in the recently established Greek state produced a lot of new buildings, but little architectural theory. Academically trained architects in Athens may have been too busy designing, or too antagonistic and secretive, to share their theories in writing. But architectural criticism abounded in the popular press, often penned by anonymous authors and frequently satirical. On February 3, 1854, the Athenian newspaper Athena (Αθηνά) published an anonymous satirical text titled “A Dialogue between the Belfries of the Capital [Διάλογος των κωδωνοστασίων της Πρωτευούσης]”. 5 In it, the belfries of Athens’ churches debate current affairs and the future of the city, acutely aware of the shifting geopolitics of Europe.

Athens had become the Greek capital two decades earlier, and was the epicentre of intensive building activity. Plans were drawn up to rebuild it on a rectangular grid and expand it on monumental axes. 6 Its ancient sites were cleared of rubble and anything else that was seen as an obstruction, including Byzantine and Ottoman remains. 7 Monumental neoclassical buildings were erected to house the country’s new institutions: a university, an academy, a library, a palace . . . The small Ottoman town of Athens was trying to transform itself into a European capital.

Theophil Hansen’s 1859 watercolour plan for The Athenian Trilogy on Panepistimiou Avenue. Hansen was commissioned by King Otto to design the National Library of Greece (left), University of Athens (centre), and Academy of Athens (right). The buildings were completed, respectively, in 1903, 1864, and 1887 — Source .

Given this aspiration, it is fitting that the “Dialogue” opens with the belfry of the Byzantine church of Taxiarchs, a modest eleventh-century chapel that stood next to the Roman Agora and would in later years be demolished, 8 boasting with great confidence:

> All the travellers that pass by here fix their eyes on me and admire me. Many say that, in the whole world, there are only three belfries worth talking about: the one of [Our Lady of] Tinos, the one of [the Cathedral of] Strasbourg, and me . . . . And I do not say this out of any vanity — the other day I saw an [English] lord who not only observed me with great curiosity, but also cried in admiration: “By Zeus! This belfry is worthy of being transported to the British Museum!” . . . What other building has ever heard such praise from the Enlightened world? 9

In reality, few foreign travellers (whether onlookers or looters) or local authorities were interested in Greece’s Byzantine churches at that time. 10 Systematic efforts for their protection would begin toward the end of the nineteenth century, 11 but initially, these buildings received little attention, 12 despite the ostensible existence of a law ordering the preservation of the Byzantine, Venetian, and Turkish “relics of the Middle Ages”. 13 Many of these churches were left in disrepair or demolished to make way for new streets and buildings, 14 or even reclaimed as material for the construction of new churches. 15 A survey of Athens in 1833 documented a total of 115 churches, of which only 30 were deemed in a good enough condition to merit repairs; a survey made roughly a decade later indicated that only half of those survived. 16

Pierre Peytier’s drawing of the Fethiye Mosque and the Church of the Taxiarchs in Athens, ca. 1830s — Source .

André Couchaud’s architectural drawings of the Church of the Taxiarchs, from Choix d’églises bysantines en Grèce (1842) — Source .

The Taxiarchs belfry’s braggadocio was ironic, of course, because like all the rest of post-Ottoman Athens’ churches, it was modest at best. Views of the city around 1800 — such as Edward Dodwell’s famous image of The Bazaar at Athens — show a skyline dominated by minarets, not bell towers. Christians living under Ottoman rule were only allowed to build or repair churches as long as their architecture did not compete with that of the mosques. 17 In most cases, freestanding bell towers were not allowed. The old churches of Athens only had modest belfries, usually at the extension of an existing wall, where a single bell hung under an arched opening.

Edward Dodwell, The Bazaar at Athens , ca. 1800–30 — Source .

After the withdrawal of Ottoman forces from Athens in 1833, all of the city’s minarets were gradually demolished, along with many of its mosques. In the 1840s and 50s, a number of projects for the erection of new churches or the refurbishment of existing ones began to explore new architectural possibilities, styles, and typologies, some of which involved monumental, at times freestanding bell towers. 18 It was precisely such a new construction that the belfries of the “Dialogue” were meeting to discuss.

The news is announced by the belfry of Saint Marina near Thisseion: carved into the rock of the Hill of the Nymphs, this minuscule thirteenth-century chapel was almost as obscure as the Taxiarchs, and, like it, was later demolished and replaced by a modern church. 19

Harald Conrad Stilling’s 1853 study of the Church of Agia Marina on the Hill of the Nymphs, Athens — Source .

Saint Marina interrupts the Taxiarchs:

> [Saint Marina:] Quiet down, brother, stop shouting . . . . Now comes the time when you will cease your bragging. [Taxiarchs:] What are you talking about, my insignificant little belfry? Pardon me, I was unaware of your existence. Tell me, why and for whom should I cease? [Saint Marina:] I heard . . . that a gleaming, tall and elegant belfry will soon be erected in our city. [Taxiarchs:] Where, my little one, where? And it will be tall, you say? [Saint Marina:] Yes! the old Nikodemos is planning to dazzle our eyes; he wants to make a child in his own image and likeness. Many say that this will be the most beautiful creature. [Taxiarchs:] And tall, you say? [Saint Marina:] I heard it will be tall, as tall as the sky . . . 20

“Nikodemos” [Sotira Nikodemou, also known as Lykodemou] was an eleventh-century Byzantine church, whose complete refurbishment included the erection of a new, freestanding, four-storey bell tower, then an unprecedented novelty for the city. The church had been given to Athens’ expanding Russian community after a petition from Tsar Nicholas I. It was perhaps the popularity of neo-Byzantine architecture in the Russian Empire at the time that led to the bell tower being designed in imitation of the church it neighboured. The tower, completed in 1855, imitated the church’s distinctive details, from its brick-arched windows and cloisonné masonry to its pseudo-Kufic ornament and thin strips of ceramic dentils. 21

André Couchaud’s imagined reconstruction of the front of the Church of Sotira Nikodemou, 1842 — Source .

André Couchaud’s imagined reconstruction of the side of the Church of Sotira Nikodemou, 1842 — Source .

Lithograph of the Sotira Nikodemou, Athens, printed by Lemercier & Cie., from Ethnikon Hēmerologion (1867) — Source .

Built with Russian funds, this flamboyant construction had important political implications. The Crimean War (1853–56) was in full swing, and Greece, ruled by the Bavarian-born King Otto, had found itself trapped between Europe’s Great Powers. Russia’s attack on the Ottoman Empire and its claim to defend the well-being of all Orthodox Christians living under the Sultan’s rule appealed to newly independent Greeks — some of whom were revanchists that dreamt of a Greek “reconquest” of Istanbul and the Hagia Sophia. However, England and France were applying their own pressure for Greece to withdraw. On May 12, 1854 (three months after the publication of the “Dialogue”, and while the restoration of the church was still under way), England and France occupied the port of Piraeus and the city of Athens, and forced King Otto to withdraw his troops from Ottoman territories and to declare Greece’s neutrality.

Accordingly, three less indigenous structures of Athens then join the conversation: the Clock Tower of Elgin in the Roman Agora, which was built in 1814 to accommodate a large clock gifted by Lord Elgin after he had looted the Parthenon marbles; 22 the belfry of the recently completed neo-Gothic Anglican church on Philhellenon Street; 23 and the belfry of the Catholic church of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite (“Saint Denis”) on Panepistimiou Avenue, whose slow construction had become a local joke. 24 These three buildings personified foreign interests in Greece and the various foreign communities (Germans, Austrians, French, English, and Americans) and confessions (Catholics and Protestants) that had settled in Athens after 1830 and had funded their construction. Russian presence represented a threat to all these Western powers, and so the three foreign buildings fiercely oppose the project of the bell tower of Saint Nikodemos by appealing to local patriotic sentiment.

Photograph of the Clock Tower of Elgin in the Roman Agora of Athens, ca. 1871 — Source .

Postcard of Saint Paul’s, a neo-Gothic Anglican church in Athens, by Pallis & Cotzias, ca. 1900–1906 — Source .

Postcard of the Cathedral Basilica of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, the main Roman Catholic cathedral in Athens, ca. 1910 — Source .

The Clock Tower of Elgin speaks first:

> It’s a conspiracy! Thieves, robbers! Grab your arms, brothers! friends! neighbours! Look, we are perishing! rush to the rescue! . . . For the love of God, wake up! behold . . . our enemy . . . he is approaching, he is here... he captures us, he murders! 25

The belfries of the Anglican church and Saint Denis join the chorus:

> Do not let him approach!

When one of the local belfries asks them who that incoming enemy is, the Clock Tower of Elgin declares:

> It’s the Moscov Giaour [sic: Ο Μοσκόβ Γκιαούρ]. 26

The Turkish word “giaour [gâvur]” was a derogatory Ottoman term for a non-Muslim, particularly a Christian. By putting this word in the mouth of the English tower, the author of the “Dialogue” hints at the true allegiance of these Western powers: not to the Greeks, whom they called “brothers” a moment ago, but to the Sultan.

For many Greek elites and the Bavarian-born monarchy, maintaining the alliance with these Western powers was a priority — Athens’ foreign communities needed to be accommodated. But the erection of new Protestant and Catholic churches was an affront to the local Orthodox population, who were receiving no new church of their own. In 1841, an anonymous newspaper columnist condemned “the unforgivable indifference” of the Greek government with regard to “building an [Orthodox] church . . . with sufficient capacity and the needed propriety” for official celebrations. 27 Adding insult to injury, King Otto himself had remained Catholic on taking the throne. Although he attended Orthodox celebrations and even sponsored the erection of the city’s Metropolitan Cathedral (which would be completed in 1862), he had not received an Orthodox baptism. This did not sit well with many of his Greek subjects.

In this context, the pompous restoration of an old Byzantine church by the Orthodox Tsar of Russia would have certainly been welcomed by many Athenians — perhaps even by the anonymous author of the “Dialogue”. Still, all the Orthodox churches of the “Dialogue” do not form a unified front. The churches are riven by internal divides. Soon after the appearance of the two old Byzantine churches and the three Western structures, a modern Orthodox church enters the scene: Saint Eirini. Completed just four years earlier and serving at the time as the city’s Orthodox cathedral, Saint Eirini was a gleaming neo-Renaissance edifice, whose plastered and pedimented facade stood on one of the city’s first monumental avenues, Aiolou Street. Like the other Athenian churches, however, Saint Eirini lacked big bell towers: its bells hung on two relatively modest belfries over its facade. And so it also regards the new Russian bell tower with envy.

Detail from a photograph of Athens, taken from the Acropolis, with Saint Eirini at its centre, published in Recueil de photographies d’Athènes et ses antiquités, offert au prince impérial (Collection of Photographs of Athens and Its Antiquities, Presented to the Prince Imperial), ca. 1858–59 — Source .

Ultimately, it is not confession but architectural form that determines the battle lines. When the Byzantine chapel of the Transfiguration of the Saviour at the foot of the Acropolis joins the chorus against the Russian tower, Saint Eirini scoffs:

> What? You too . . . are speaking against [this tower]? When we say something against Nikodemos, anyone can easily conclude [that this stems] from our Italian character . . . but you, have you no shame? Both in name and in essence [ονόματι και πράγματι], you are truly a Russian belfry. 28

For the neo-Renaissance Saint Eirini, the Byzantine architecture of this little chapel of the Transfiguration puts it in the same camp as Nikodemos. Many similar accusations were made in the “Dialogue”. When the neo-Gothic Anglican church joins the neo-Renaissance Saint Denis in shooing away their common enemy, the Byzantine church of Saint Marina accuses the former: “You have nothing in common with Saint Denis. You have our [i.e., Byzantine] form and, together with your church, you face the east [Συ και το σχήμα ημέτερον έχεις και μετά της εκκλησίας σου προς ανατολάς στρέφεις]”. 29 The confusion in the accusations appears to be intentional: the author of the “Dialogue” was satirizing the chaos in the city around the classification of historical architectural styles, typologies, and genealogies. 30

Étienne Rey, Mur septentrional de l’Acropole d’Athènes , chalcograph showing the northern wall of the Acropolis and the Church of the Transfiguration (Metamorfosi Sotiros), drawn in 1843 and published in 1867 — Source .

In the newly established Greek nation-state, whose nation-building discourse was almost exclusively based on classical antiquity, medieval diversions were often a matter of controversy. As Greek nation-builders were anxious to construct a narrative of uninterrupted continuity with classical antiquity in order to align themselves with the West, Byzantium was seen by many as a “dark”, “oriental” interval that was best left forgotten. However, King Otto was occasionally favourable to modern uses of the local Byzantine heritage. In 1846, he launched a competition for the design of the Athens Metropolitan Cathedral and urged that it be done in a “Greco-Byzantine [Ελληνοβυζαντινό]” style. 31 The winning design, by local architect Demetrios Zezos — a mixture of Byzantine, Romanesque, and classicist features — was lauded by some 32 but loathed by others; one enraged anonymous author wrote in an Athenian newspaper in 1857:

> What a shame [for one] to see such architectural monstrosities [εξαμβλώματα αρχιτεκτονικής], such testaments of utter tastelessness. And where? In the city of Athens, next to the Propylaea, the Parthenon and the Erechtheion! It seems that we are trying to surpass the Byzantines in tastelessness, instead of using as our models the wonderful works of our immortal forefathers [i.e., the ancient Greeks]. 33

As the “Dialogue” unfolds, all these modern churches of Athens (both those of Western confessions and those in Western styles) eventually stop accusing each other and unite against Nikodemos, scrutinizing its architecture for incriminating details they could use to stop the construction. The first thing they notice is the orientation of the new structure. The tower had been placed parallel to the old church, which, like most older buildings, did not align with the new urban grid that was built around them. As a result, the Anglican church points out, the bell tower stood more or less at a 45-degree angle to the adjacent Philhellenon Street.

André Couchaud, Église de St. Nicodème , an architectural drawing of the church before its restoration and the addition of the bell tower, from Choix d’églises bysantines en Grèce (Selected Byzantine Churches in Greece), 1842 — Source .

Photograph of the bell tower of Sotira Nikodemou and, further down the street, Saint Paul’s, in Athens, ca. 1900 — Source .

Yet they need more. Saint Eirini takes the lead, assuming a prosecutorial tone:

> By God, why [should there be] such a tall belfry in our small and poor capital? What is the use for it? What are we, Turks, wanting minarets? [Μη γαρ ημείς Τούρκοι είμεθα και θέλομεν μιναρέδας;] . . . The ancient and sacred Acropolis is indignant about this sacrilegious novelty, and [Mount] Hymettus, from his top to his lowest foothills, has likely the same opinion. 34

This is still not enough, so Saint Eirini continues:

> My brothers and partners, you know that this monster has sprouted out of the ground like a mushroom, without following any kind of architecture, and stands, as is known, before the entrance of Nikodemos. It is also known that Hagia Sophia [in Istanbul] had her belfry placed similarly before her, but . . . why should we care about this Turkish mosque [τι μέλλει ημίν δια το Τουρκικόν αυτό τζαμίον]? The Queen of churches and the model for our Metropolitan Cathedral — that is, Saint Peter’s [in Rome] — has his facade open and free [of any such obstacles]. And so we all cry out that this monstrosity of Nikodemos is an inexcusable disproportion, a rape and an infection of the ancient Byzantine architecture — deafness, barbarism, nonsense, treachery ...chery ...ery ...ry , etc. [προδοσία ...σία ...ία ...α , κτλ]. 35

The echo of the last word — “προδοσία ...σία ...ία ...α ” — adds to the comic effect, as we imagine Saint Eirini pompously rehearsing its speech in an empty hall. The addition of “etc.” at the end hints at the banality of it all despite the urgent tone: one can easily imagine the rest, the author of the “Dialogue” implies.

But something more interesting is taking place here: Saint Eirini brings in Hagia Sophia — an object of profound religious veneration and nationalist desire for most Greeks — but only to dismiss it as a “Turkish mosque”, and then to turn the audience’s attention to Saint Peter’s in Rome, which it deems the true model for the Metropolitan Cathedral of Athens (at the time under construction), even though the latter had evident Byzantine and Gothic features. As it mounts its argument, Saint Eirini often distorts historical facts but is consistent in embracing Western architectural models and in its fiery rejection of anything “oriental”.

Suddenly, a mysterious new character appears: the “Ideal Belfry [Κωδωνοστάσιον Ιδανικόν]” 36 , which interrupts the conversation with the “most cunning” and “devilish idea”:

> [we should say that] this newly sprouted monster is a mere reflection [i.e., reversal] of the Western belfry type, and that this [reflection] was born out of an infantile rivalry . . . that is: because our Saint Denis (against the rules of Western architecture) will have his belfry in his rear side, 37 Saint Nikodemos [decided that he] has to have his in the front. Is this not ridiculous? . . . Don’t you think that this amazing idea of mine will bring the great result that we are all striving for? Won’t this choke the foetus in the womb, and thus halt the plan of the Russian? 38

Here the argument is completely reversed: while Saint Eirini has been focusing on Nikodemos’ supposed Turkishness, the Ideal Belfry argues that it is instead an imitation, or rather a superficial reaction to, Western-style building. The accusation does not entirely make sense, but the other belfries burst out in triumphant laughter and congratulate the Ideal Belfry.

Eugène Viollet-le-Duc’s rendering of the bell tower of Saint-Front, Périgueux, from his Dictionnaire raisonné de l’architecture française , vol. 3 (1875 edition). Viollet-le-Duc regarded this tower, with its Romanesque and Byzantine features, as a prototype for the bell towers of western France — Source .

Eugène Viollet-le-Duc’s map tracing the geographical diffusion of bell tower prototypes in France by the mid-twelfth century, from the same volume — Source .

The “Dialogue” ends with a twist: the introduction of the “ancient belfries [αρχαία κωδωνοστάσια] of Athens”, i.e., those of the city’s Byzantine churches. These elders put an end to the plot of all the newly or not-yet-built churches and defend Nikodemos:

> We have known the Russian for nine centuries, and have seen him in many different circumstances up until the present one; but we have never seen envy or rivalry in him, apart from a feeling of shame in the face of secret plans for the destruction of humanity. Petty for the petty, stupid for the stupid, and foul for the foul. [Τα μικρά τοις μικροίς, τα μωρά τοις μωροίς και τα αισχρά τοις αισχροίς.] So, petty one, hide away your stupid and foul invention. 39

This ending makes it clear that the author of the “Dialogue” approved of the new project of the bell tower. What is already evident is that they disapproved of the criticisms levelled against it and the inconclusive debates about architectural style in nineteenth-century Athens. The author’s identity remains unknown: the text is only signed with the letter “S. [Σ.]”, preceded by an obscure note:

> Having accidentally found this dialogue written on an ancient piece of paper with modern letters [i.e., modern language], I publish it for the sake of curiosity [and] to make it known to all belfries. 40

The author’s mention of “modern letters” on “ancient paper” reads like a satirical reference to another great debate of the time: the “Greek language question”, about whether the language of modern Greece ought to be the commonly spoken vernacular or a cultivated literary language modelled on ancient Greek. But the note also reads like a cautious (albeit joking) denial of authorship. The fact that this author felt the urge to publish their text anonymously, and to disguise their opinion as the voice of the city’s “ancient belfries”, is indicative of the tense atmosphere of Athens in the middle of the nineteenth century.

More than a piece of architectural criticism, the “Dialogue” was a symptom of the anxieties of Greek nation-building, which the Crimean War intensified: to establish a modern state and maintain alliances with Western powers, a clear connection with the classical past had to be enforced on a country whose history was marked by centuries of Byzantine and Ottoman culture as well as Christian Orthodox alliances. Medieval and vernacular architecture, which for many in the West served as the foundation of nationhood, were, in the case of Greece, highly contested. For some, Byzantium was a symbol of the local faith; for others, a source of unwanted “oriental” pedigree.

The author of the “Dialogue” was bold enough to satirize all factions involved in the political debates of the time, from the provincialism of their compatriots to the opportunism of foreign powers. And they were cautious enough to resort to anonymity and ventriloquism. At the time of the emergence of the idea of “heritage”, and as both old monuments and new projects became increasingly charged with ideological claims, one could simply let the buildings talk.

## Bickering Buildings A Dialogue Between the Churches of Athens in 1854

The churches of Athens had much to say in 1854, when an anonymous author staged a squabble between them in newsprint. Nikos Magouliotis eavesdrops on this chatter, finding personified anxieties about Greek architectural identity, foreign influence, and the newly formed nation’s relation to its past.

Published

November 24, 2026

Gabriel de Rumine’s 1858 photograph of Athens from the Acropolis. The Metropolitan Cathedral is under construction in the foreground — Source .

Buildings are often thought of as “silent witnesses of history”, but they have a history of talking, especially in moments of crisis. In a pamphlet published in London in 1641, at the height of the Reformation, two monuments that served as sites of Catholic devotion literally converse, trying to make sense of (and poke fun at) the Protestant vandalism against them. 1 In the eighteenth century, a whole genre of texts developed in which authors imagined what buildings might have said if they could speak to each other or passersby. 2

This was not just a matter for the popular press. The end of the eighteenth century saw the emergence of “architecture parlante” (speaking architecture), through a group of architects who argued that buildings ought to communicate their function and meaning to people, through figurative symbols, letters, or inscriptions. 3 When opinions about a certain monument or a cityscape predominate, buildings must speak for themselves to set things straight. This happened through experimental designs by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux and others, but also through pamphlets, broadsheets, cartoons, and newspaper articles that were written for a broader public and gave voice to the built environment. 4

In mid-nineteenth-century Athens, the furious construction of the new capital in the recently established Greek state produced a lot of new buildings, but little architectural theory. Academically trained architects in Athens may have been too busy designing, or too antagonistic and secretive, to share their theories in writing. But architectural criticism abounded in the popular press, often penned by anonymous authors and frequently satirical. On February 3, 1854, the Athenian newspaper Athena (Αθηνά) published an anonymous satirical text titled “A Dialogue between the Belfries of the Capital [Διάλογος των κωδωνοστασίων της Πρωτευούσης]”. 5 In it, the belfries of Athens’ churches debate current affairs and the future of the city, acutely aware of the shifting geopolitics of Europe.

Athens had become the Greek capital two decades earlier, and was the epicentre of intensive building activity. Plans were drawn up to rebuild it on a rectangular grid and expand it on monumental axes. 6 Its ancient sites were cleared of rubble and anything else that was seen as an obstruction, including Byzantine and Ottoman remains. 7 Monumental neoclassical buildings were erected to house the country’s new institutions: a university, an academy, a library, a palace . . . The small Ottoman town of Athens was trying to transform itself into a European capital.

Theophil Hansen’s 1859 watercolour plan for The Athenian Trilogy on Panepistimiou Avenue. Hansen was commissioned by King Otto to design the National Library of Greece (left), University of Athens (centre), and Academy of Athens (right). The buildings were completed, respectively, in 1903, 1864, and 1887 — Source .

Given this aspiration, it is fitting that the “Dialogue” opens with the belfry of the Byzantine church of Taxiarchs, a modest eleventh-century chapel that stood next to the Roman Agora and would in later years be demolished, 8 boasting with great confidence:

> All the travellers that pass by here fix their eyes on me and admire me. Many say that, in the whole world, there are only three belfries worth talking about: the one of [Our Lady of] Tinos, the one of [the Cathedral of] Strasbourg, and me . . . . And I do not say this out of any vanity — the other day I saw an [English] lord who not only observed me with great curiosity, but also cried in admiration: “By Zeus! This belfry is worthy of being transported to the British Museum!” . . . What other building has ever heard such praise from the Enlightened world? 9

In reality, few foreign travellers (whether onlookers or looters) or local authorities were interested in Greece’s Byzantine churches at that time. 10 Systematic efforts for their protection would begin toward the end of the nineteenth century, 11 but initially, these buildings received little attention, 12 despite the ostensible existence of a law ordering the preservation of the Byzantine, Venetian, and Turkish “relics of the Middle Ages”. 13 Many of these churches were left in disrepair or demolished to make way for new streets and buildings, 14 or even reclaimed as material for the construction of new churches. 15 A survey of Athens in 1833 documented a total of 115 churches, of which only 30 were deemed in a good enough condition to merit repairs; a survey made roughly a decade later indicated that only half of those survived. 16

Pierre Peytier’s drawing of the Fethiye Mosque and the Church of the Taxiarchs in Athens, ca. 1830s — Source .

André Couchaud’s architectural drawings of the Church of the Taxiarchs, from Choix d’églises bysantines en Grèce (1842) — Source .

The Taxiarchs belfry’s braggadocio was ironic, of course, because like all the rest of post-Ottoman Athens’ churches, it was modest at best. Views of the city around 1800 — such as Edward Dodwell’s famous image of The Bazaar at Athens — show a skyline dominated by minarets, not bell towers. Christians living under Ottoman rule were only allowed to build or repair churches as long as their architecture did not compete with that of the mosques. 17 In most cases, freestanding bell towers were not allowed. The old churches of Athens only had modest belfries, usually at the extension of an existing wall, where a single bell hung under an arched opening.

Edward Dodwell, The Bazaar at Athens , ca. 1800–30 — Source .

After the withdrawal of Ottoman forces from Athens in 1833, all of the city’s minarets were gradually demolished, along with many of its mosques. In the 1840s and 50s, a number of projects for the erection of new churches or the refurbishment of existing ones began to explore new architectural possibilities, styles, and typologies, some of which involved monumental, at times freestanding bell towers. 18 It was precisely such a new construction that the belfries of the “Dialogue” were meeting to discuss.

The news is announced by the belfry of Saint Marina near Thisseion: carved into the rock of the Hill of the Nymphs, this minuscule thirteenth-century chapel was almost as obscure as the Taxiarchs, and, like it, was later demolished and replaced by a modern church. 19

Harald Conrad Stilling’s 1853 study of the Church of Agia Marina on the Hill of the Nymphs, Athens — Source .

Saint Marina interrupts the Taxiarchs:

> [Saint Marina:] Quiet down, brother, stop shouting . . . . Now comes the time when you will cease your bragging. [Taxiarchs:] What are you talking about, my insignificant little belfry? Pardon me, I was unaware of your existence. Tell me, why and for whom should I cease? [Saint Marina:] I heard . . . that a gleaming, tall and elegant belfry will soon be erected in our city. [Taxiarchs:] Where, my little one, where? And it will be tall, you say? [Saint Marina:] Yes! the old Nikodemos is planning to dazzle our eyes; he wants to make a child in his own image and likeness. Many say that this will be the most beautiful creature. [Taxiarchs:] And tall, you say? [Saint Marina:] I heard it will be tall, as tall as the sky . . . 20

“Nikodemos” [Sotira Nikodemou, also known as Lykodemou] was an eleventh-century Byzantine church, whose complete refurbishment included the erection of a new, freestanding, four-storey bell tower, then an unprecedented novelty for the city. The church had been given to Athens’ expanding Russian community after a petition from Tsar Nicholas I. It was perhaps the popularity of neo-Byzantine architecture in the Russian Empire at the time that led to the bell tower being designed in imitation of the church it neighboured. The tower, completed in 1855, imitated the church’s distinctive details, from its brick-arched windows and cloisonné masonry to its pseudo-Kufic ornament and thin strips of ceramic dentils. 21

André Couchaud’s imagined reconstruction of the front of the Church of Sotira Nikodemou, 1842 — Source .

André Couchaud’s imagined reconstruction of the side of the Church of Sotira Nikodemou, 1842 — Source .

Lithograph of the Sotira Nikodemou, Athens, printed by Lemercier & Cie., from Ethnikon Hēmerologion (1867) — Source .

Built with Russian funds, this flamboyant construction had important political implications. The Crimean War (1853–56) was in full swing, and Greece, ruled by the Bavarian-born King Otto, had found itself trapped between Europe’s Great Powers. Russia’s attack on the Ottoman Empire and its claim to defend the well-being of all Orthodox Christians living under the Sultan’s rule appealed to newly independent Greeks — some of whom were revanchists that dreamt of a Greek “reconquest” of Istanbul and the Hagia Sophia. However, England and France were applying their own pressure for Greece to withdraw. On May 12, 1854 (three months after the publication of the “Dialogue”, and while the restoration of the church was still under way), England and France occupied the port of Piraeus and the city of Athens, and forced King Otto to withdraw his troops from Ottoman territories and to declare Greece’s neutrality.

Accordingly, three less indigenous structures of Athens then join the conversation: the Clock Tower of Elgin in the Roman Agora, which was built in 1814 to accommodate a large clock gifted by Lord Elgin after he had looted the Parthenon marbles; 22 the belfry of the recently completed neo-Gothic Anglican church on Philhellenon Street; 23 and the belfry of the Catholic church of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite (“Saint Denis”) on Panepistimiou Avenue, whose slow construction had become a local joke. 24 These three buildings personified foreign interests in Greece and the various foreign communities (Germans, Austrians, French, English, and Americans) and confessions (Catholics and Protestants) that had settled in Athens after 1830 and had funded their construction. Russian presence represented a threat to all these Western powers, and so the three foreign buildings fiercely oppose the project of the bell tower of Saint Nikodemos by appealing to local patriotic sentiment.

Photograph of the Clock Tower of Elgin in the Roman Agora of Athens, ca. 1871 — Source .

Postcard of Saint Paul’s, a neo-Gothic Anglican church in Athens, by Pallis & Cotzias, ca. 1900–1906 — Source .

Postcard of the Cathedral Basilica of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, the main Roman Catholic cathedral in Athens, ca. 1910 — Source .

The Clock Tower of Elgin speaks first:

> It’s a conspiracy! Thieves, robbers! Grab your arms, brothers! friends! neighbours! Look, we are perishing! rush to the rescue! . . . For the love of God, wake up! behold . . . our enemy . . . he is approaching, he is here... he captures us, he murders! 25

The belfries of the Anglican church and Saint Denis join the chorus:

> Do not let him approach!

When one of the local belfries asks them who that incoming enemy is, the Clock Tower of Elgin declares:

> It’s the Moscov Giaour [sic: Ο Μοσκόβ Γκιαούρ]. 26

The Turkish word “giaour [gâvur]” was a derogatory Ottoman term for a non-Muslim, particularly a Christian. By putting this word in the mouth of the English tower, the author of the “Dialogue” hints at the true allegiance of these Western powers: not to the Greeks, whom they called “brothers” a moment ago, but to the Sultan.

For many Greek elites and the Bavarian-born monarchy, maintaining the alliance with these Western powers was a priority — Athens’ foreign communities needed to be accommodated. But the erection of new Protestant and Catholic churches was an affront to the local Orthodox population, who were receiving no new church of their own. In 1841, an anonymous newspaper columnist condemned “the unforgivable indifference” of the Greek government with regard to “building an [Orthodox] church . . . with sufficient capacity and the needed propriety” for official celebrations. 27 Adding insult to injury, King Otto himself had remained Catholic on taking the throne. Although he attended Orthodox celebrations and even sponsored the erection of the city’s Metropolitan Cathedral (which would be completed in 1862), he had not received an Orthodox baptism. This did not sit well with many of his Greek subjects.

In this context, the pompous restoration of an old Byzantine church by the Orthodox Tsar of Russia would have certainly been welcomed by many Athenians — perhaps even by the anonymous author of the “Dialogue”. Still, all the Orthodox churches of the “Dialogue” do not form a unified front. The churches are riven by internal divides. Soon after the appearance of the two old Byzantine churches and the three Western structures, a modern Orthodox church enters the scene: Saint Eirini. Completed just four years earlier and serving at the time as the city’s Orthodox cathedral, Saint Eirini was a gleaming neo-Renaissance edifice, whose plastered and pedimented facade stood on one of the city’s first monumental avenues, Aiolou Street. Like the other Athenian churches, however, Saint Eirini lacked big bell towers: its bells hung on two relatively modest belfries over its facade. And so it also regards the new Russian bell tower with envy.

Detail from a photograph of Athens, taken from the Acropolis, with Saint Eirini at its centre, published in Recueil de photographies d’Athènes et ses antiquités, offert au prince impérial (Collection of Photographs of Athens and Its Antiquities, Presented to the Prince Imperial), ca. 1858–59 — Source .

Ultimately, it is not confession but architectural form that determines the battle lines. When the Byzantine chapel of the Transfiguration of the Saviour at the foot of the Acropolis joins the chorus against the Russian tower, Saint Eirini scoffs:

> What? You too . . . are speaking against [this tower]? When we say something against Nikodemos, anyone can easily conclude [that this stems] from our Italian character . . . but you, have you no shame? Both in name and in essence [ονόματι και πράγματι], you are truly a Russian belfry. 28

For the neo-Renaissance Saint Eirini, the Byzantine architecture of this little chapel of the Transfiguration puts it in the same camp as Nikodemos. Many similar accusations were made in the “Dialogue”. When the neo-Gothic Anglican church joins the neo-Renaissance Saint Denis in shooing away their common enemy, the Byzantine church of Saint Marina accuses the former: “You have nothing in common with Saint Denis. You have our [i.e., Byzantine] form and, together with your church, you face the east [Συ και το σχήμα ημέτερον έχεις και μετά της εκκλησίας σου προς ανατολάς στρέφεις]”. 29 The confusion in the accusations appears to be intentional: the author of the “Dialogue” was satirizing the chaos in the city around the classification of historical architectural styles, typologies, and genealogies. 30

Étienne Rey, Mur septentrional de l’Acropole d’Athènes , chalcograph showing the northern wall of the Acropolis and the Church of the Transfiguration (Metamorfosi Sotiros), drawn in 1843 and published in 1867 — Source .

In the newly established Greek nation-state, whose nation-building discourse was almost exclusively based on classical antiquity, medieval diversions were often a matter of controversy. As Greek nation-builders were anxious to construct a narrative of uninterrupted continuity with classical antiquity in order to align themselves with the West, Byzantium was seen by many as a “dark”, “oriental” interval that was best left forgotten. However, King Otto was occasionally favourable to modern uses of the local Byzantine heritage. In 1846, he launched a competition for the design of the Athens Metropolitan Cathedral and urged that it be done in a “Greco-Byzantine [Ελληνοβυζαντινό]” style. 31 The winning design, by local architect Demetrios Zezos — a mixture of Byzantine, Romanesque, and classicist features — was lauded by some 32 but loathed by others; one enraged anonymous author wrote in an Athenian newspaper in 1857:

> What a shame [for one] to see such architectural monstrosities [εξαμβλώματα αρχιτεκτονικής], such testaments of utter tastelessness. And where? In the city of Athens, next to the Propylaea, the Parthenon and the Erechtheion! It seems that we are trying to surpass the Byzantines in tastelessness, instead of using as our models the wonderful works of our immortal forefathers [i.e., the ancient Greeks]. 33

As the “Dialogue” unfolds, all these modern churches of Athens (both those of Western confessions and those in Western styles) eventually stop accusing each other and unite against Nikodemos, scrutinizing its architecture for incriminating details they could use to stop the construction. The first thing they notice is the orientation of the new structure. The tower had been placed parallel to the old church, which, like most older buildings, did not align with the new urban grid that was built around them. As a result, the Anglican church points out, the bell tower stood more or less at a 45-degree angle to the adjacent Philhellenon Street.

André Couchaud, Église de St. Nicodème , an architectural drawing of the church before its restoration and the addition of the bell tower, from Choix d’églises bysantines en Grèce (Selected Byzantine Churches in Greece), 1842 — Source .

Photograph of the bell tower of Sotira Nikodemou and, further down the street, Saint Paul’s, in Athens, ca. 1900 — Source .

Yet they need more. Saint Eirini takes the lead, assuming a prosecutorial tone:

> By God, why [should there be] such a tall belfry in our small and poor capital? What is the use for it? What are we, Turks, wanting minarets? [Μη γαρ ημείς Τούρκοι είμεθα και θέλομεν μιναρέδας;] . . . The ancient and sacred Acropolis is indignant about this sacrilegious novelty, and [Mount] Hymettus, from his top to his lowest foothills, has likely the same opinion. 34

This is still not enough, so Saint Eirini continues:

> My brothers and partners, you know that this monster has sprouted out of the ground like a mushroom, without following any kind of architecture, and stands, as is known, before the entrance of Nikodemos. It is also known that Hagia Sophia [in Istanbul] had her belfry placed similarly before her, but . . . why should we care about this Turkish mosque [τι μέλλει ημίν δια το Τουρκικόν αυτό τζαμίον]? The Queen of churches and the model for our Metropolitan Cathedral — that is, Saint Peter’s [in Rome] — has his facade open and free [of any such obstacles]. And so we all cry out that this monstrosity of Nikodemos is an inexcusable disproportion, a rape and an infection of the ancient Byzantine architecture — deafness, barbarism, nonsense, treachery ...chery ...ery ...ry , etc. [προδοσία ...σία ...ία ...α , κτλ]. 35

The echo of the last word — “προδοσία ...σία ...ία ...α ” — adds to the comic effect, as we imagine Saint Eirini pompously rehearsing its speech in an empty hall. The addition of “etc.” at the end hints at the banality of it all despite the urgent tone: one can easily imagine the rest, the author of the “Dialogue” implies.

But something more interesting is taking place here: Saint Eirini brings in Hagia Sophia — an object of profound religious veneration and nationalist desire for most Greeks — but only to dismiss it as a “Turkish mosque”, and then to turn the audience’s attention to Saint Peter’s in Rome, which it deems the true model for the Metropolitan Cathedral of Athens (at the time under construction), even though the latter had evident Byzantine and Gothic features. As it mounts its argument, Saint Eirini often distorts historical facts but is consistent in embracing Western architectural models and in its fiery rejection of anything “oriental”.

Suddenly, a mysterious new character appears: the “Ideal Belfry [Κωδωνοστάσιον Ιδανικόν]” 36 , which interrupts the conversation with the “most cunning” and “devilish idea”:

> [we should say that] this newly sprouted monster is a mere reflection [i.e., reversal] of the Western belfry type, and that this [reflection] was born out of an infantile rivalry . . . that is: because our Saint Denis (against the rules of Western architecture) will have his belfry in his rear side, 37 Saint Nikodemos [decided that he] has to have his in the front. Is this not ridiculous? . . . Don’t you think that this amazing idea of mine will bring the great result that we are all striving for? Won’t this choke the foetus in the womb, and thus halt the plan of the Russian? 38

Here the argument is completely reversed: while Saint Eirini has been focusing on Nikodemos’ supposed Turkishness, the Ideal Belfry argues that it is instead an imitation, or rather a superficial reaction to, Western-style building. The accusation does not entirely make sense, but the other belfries burst out in triumphant laughter and congratulate the Ideal Belfry.

Eugène Viollet-le-Duc’s rendering of the bell tower of Saint-Front, Périgueux, from his Dictionnaire raisonné de l’architecture française , vol. 3 (1875 edition). Viollet-le-Duc regarded this tower, with its Romanesque and Byzantine features, as a prototype for the bell towers of western France — Source .

Eugène Viollet-le-Duc’s map tracing the geographical diffusion of bell tower prototypes in France by the mid-twelfth century, from the same volume — Source .

The “Dialogue” ends with a twist: the introduction of the “ancient belfries [αρχαία κωδωνοστάσια] of Athens”, i.e., those of the city’s Byzantine churches. These elders put an end to the plot of all the newly or not-yet-built churches and defend Nikodemos:

> We have known the Russian for nine centuries, and have seen him in many different circumstances up until the present one; but we have never seen envy or rivalry in him, apart from a feeling of shame in the face of secret plans for the destruction of humanity. Petty for the petty, stupid for the stupid, and foul for the foul. [Τα μικρά τοις μικροίς, τα μωρά τοις μωροίς και τα αισχρά τοις αισχροίς.] So, petty one, hide away your stupid and foul invention. 39

This ending makes it clear that the author of the “Dialogue” approved of the new project of the bell tower. What is already evident is that they disapproved of the criticisms levelled against it and the inconclusive debates about architectural style in nineteenth-century Athens. The author’s identity remains unknown: the text is only signed with the letter “S. [Σ.]”, preceded by an obscure note:

> Having accidentally found this dialogue written on an ancient piece of paper with modern letters [i.e., modern language], I publish it for the sake of curiosity [and] to make it known to all belfries. 40

The author’s mention of “modern letters” on “ancient paper” reads like a satirical reference to another great debate of the time: the “Greek language question”, about whether the language of modern Greece ought to be the commonly spoken vernacular or a cultivated literary language modelled on ancient Greek. But the note also reads like a cautious (albeit joking) denial of authorship. The fact that this author felt the urge to publish their text anonymously, and to disguise their opinion as the voice of the city’s “ancient belfries”, is indicative of the tense atmosphere of Athens in the middle of the nineteenth century.

More than a piece of architectural criticism, the “Dialogue” was a symptom of the anxieties of Greek nation-building, which the Crimean War intensified: to establish a modern state and maintain alliances with Western powers, a clear connection with the classical past had to be enforced on a country whose history was marked by centuries of Byzantine and Ottoman culture as well as Christian Orthodox alliances. Medieval and vernacular architecture, which for many in the West served as the foundation of nationhood, were, in the case of Greece, highly contested. For some, Byzantium was a symbol of the local faith; for others, a source of unwanted “oriental” pedigree.

The author of the “Dialogue” was bold enough to satirize all factions involved in the political debates of the time, from the provincialism of their compatriots to the opportunism of foreign powers. And they were cautious enough to resort to anonymity and ventriloquism. At the time of the emergence of the idea of “heritage”, and as both old monuments and new projects became increasingly charged with ideological claims, one could simply let the buildings talk.

- Byzantine Athens, 10th–12th Centuries By Charalambos Bouras In this masterful synthesis, Charalambos Bouras draws together material and textual evidence for Athens in the Middle Byzantine period, from the mid-tenth century to 1204, when it was conquered by Crusaders. What emerges from his meticulous investigation is an urban fabric surprisingly makeshift in its domestic sector yet exuberantly creative in its ecclesiastical architecture. Rather than viewing the city as a mere shadow of its ancient past, Bouras demonstrates how Athens remained an important city of the Byzantine Empire as the seat of a metropolitan, home to local aristocracy, and pilgrimage destination for those who came to worship at the Christian Parthenon. Dr. Nikos Magouliotis is an architectural historian and lecturer at ETH Zurich. His research focuses on the intersections between architecture, popular culture, archaeology, and ethnography in the east Mediterranean and in Central Europe. He has published articles in magazines such as San Rocco , ARCH+ , and Platform Space , as well as papers in the following academic journals: Architectural Histories , Future Anterior , The Journal of Architecture , Architecture Beyond Europe , and OASE .

articleBody:
In a Buddhist temple in the northeast of Thailand, not far from the border with Laos, one can find the World's Only Dinosaur Pulpit.

Located in the city of Khon Kean, the fourth-largest city in Thailand and the heart of the Isan region, the pulpit can be found inside the Buddhist temple Wat That Phra Aram Luang. If you look closely, you'll notice there are dinosaur mural paintings on the walls inside the temple as well.

Having been the site of Thailand’s first dinosaur fossil discovery, Khon Kean boasts a variety of dinosaur-related sites. Dinosaur imagery is scattered throughout the entire region, giving a nod to this history. Among these references is the World's Only Dinosaur pulpit. The pulpit is shaped like a giant Phuwiangosaurus, Thailand’s native sauropod dinosaur. The dinosaur was originally discovered in the hills of Phu Wiang outside the city, and officially named in 1994 in honor of Her Royal Highness Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn.

Monks reportedly stand inside the dinosaur to give sermons at times. Wat That Phra Aram Luang temple is a stunning sight to behold on its own, resplendent with numerous golden peaks and facades painted in bright shades or red.
