body:
Der Digitalpakt 2.0 ist gestartet, doch in vielen Ländern stehen die Förderrichtlinien noch aus. Was sollten Schulen und Schulträger jetzt tun? Livia Brenner, Projektleiterin Förderprogramme der Digitalakademie von Converge Germany, über die Lehren aus dem ersten Digitalpakt, die Rolle der Fortbildung und den Wert einer ehrlichen Bestandsaufnahme.

**Frau Brenner, der Digitalpakt 2.0 ist seit September in Kraft. Was ändert sich für Schulen und Schulträger?**

Beim ersten Digitalpakt ging es vor allem darum, die Schulen überhaupt auszustatten, also mit WLAN, Endgeräten und Präsentationstechnik. Das ist an vielen Schulen gelungen. Heute lautet die Frage eher: Wie halten wir die Technik am Laufen? Wie erneuern wir sie? Und wie kommt sie wirklich im Unterricht an?

Genau hier setzt der neue Pakt an. Bund und Länder stellen bis 2030 zusammen fünf Milliarden Euro bereit. Gefördert werden weiterhin Netzwerke, WLAN, Endgeräte und Lernplattformen. Neu dazu kommen digitale Bildungsinhalte und Software für den Unterricht. Auch der Aufbau professioneller Strukturen für Administration und Support ist förderfähig, ebenso Fortbildungen für Lehrkräfte. Außerdem sollen die Verfahren einfacher werden, etwa durch Pauschalen. Was davon Vorrang hat und wie die Verfahren konkret aussehen, entscheidet allerdings jedes Bundesland selbst.

**Das heißt, Schulen und Schulträger müssen erst einmal abwarten?**

Beim Geld ja, bei der Vorbereitung nicht. Viele Länder arbeiten noch an ihren Richtlinien. Die Zeit bis dahin lässt sich aber gut nutzen. Wer weiß, wo er steht und was er braucht, kann schnell handeln, sobald die Regeln feststehen. Wer erst dann anfängt, über seinen Bedarf nachzudenken, verliert Monate.

**Sie sprechen für die Digitalakademie von Converge Germany. Was genau macht sie?**

Die Digitalakademie ist der Fortbildungsanbieter von Converge Germany. Converge Germany selbst ist ein IT-Systemhaus und arbeitet seit mehr als 20 Jahren mit Schulen, Schulträgern und Behörden zusammen. Mit seinem 360°-Ansatz deckt das Unternehmen alles ab, von Planung und Beschaffung über die IT-Infrastruktur bis zu Service und Support im laufenden Betrieb. Wir in der Digitalakademie sorgen dafür, dass all das im Klassenzimmer ankommt.

Unser Team arbeitet bundesweit. Die Referent*innen haben einen pädagogischen oder bildungswissenschaftlichen Hintergrund, und einige haben selbst unterrichtet, ich selbst auch. Wir haben insgesamt bereits über 100.000 Lehrkräfte fortgebildet. Diese Nähe zur Praxis merkt man in jeder Fortbildung. Wir kennen den Moment, in dem 28 Augenpaare gespannt nach vorne schauen und die Technik streikt. Und wir wissen auch, dass im Lehrerzimmer selten Zeit bleibt, sich in ein neues Programm einzuarbeiten.

**Sie haben Schulen und Schulträger schon beim ersten DigitalPakt begleitet. Was haben Sie daraus gelernt?**

Vor allem eines: Ausstattung allein reicht nicht. Wir haben in den vergangenen Jahren sehr unterschiedliche Projekte umgesetzt. Für einen Kunden haben wir eine Cloud-Lösung aufgebaut, über die rund 25.000 Lehrkräfte-Geräte zentral verwaltet und abgesichert werden. Bei einem anderen haben wir das WLAN im gesamten Schulumfeld eingerichtet, ausgelegt für rund 135.000 Nutzerinnen und Nutzer.

Dabei hat sich ein Muster gezeigt. Gut lief es dort, wo Technik, Support und Fortbildung von Anfang an zusammen geplant wurden. Wo das nicht der Fall war, standen Geräte ungenutzt im Schrank – oder die Lehrkräfte wurden zu Hobby-Administratoren.

Ein Beispiel ist mir besonders im Gedächtnis geblieben. An einer Schule reichte das WLAN nicht aus, um die Updates für die iPads aufzuspielen. Eine Lehrerin hat deshalb jeden Tag Geräte aus dem iPad-Koffer mit nach Hause genommen, damit sie dort die Updates laden konnten. Das zeigt großes Engagement. Aber so etwas darf nicht die Lösung sein.

**Stichwort Fortbildung: Im Digitalpakt 2.0 ist sie förderfähig. Was bedeutet das für Schulen?**

Zunächst ist das ein wichtiges Signal. Der Pakt erkennt an, dass Technik ohne Qualifizierung wenig bewirkt. Wie die Länder Fortbildung umsetzen, ist unterschiedlich. Manche setzen stärker auf ihre Landesinstitute, andere binden externe Anbieter ein. Oft ergänzt sich beides. Wir arbeiten zum Teil auch mit Landesinstituten zusammen, etwa in Rheinland-Pfalz. Viele Schulen kommen aber direkt auf uns zu, weil sie ein Angebot suchen, das genau zu ihrer Ausstattung und ihrem Kollegium passt.

Was konkret über den Digitalpakt finanziert wird, legt jedes Land in seiner Richtlinie fest. Bis dahin lohnt es sich, den eigenen Fortbildungsbedarf zu klären. Dabei unterstützen wir Schulen und schauen gemeinsam, welche Förderwege infrage kommen. Neben dem Digitalpakt gibt es oft weitere Programme, die sich gut kombinieren lassen.

**Schauen wir auf den Unterricht selbst: Was ist beim digitalen Lehren und Lernen aus Ihrer Sicht entscheidend?**

Pädagogik und Didaktik müssen vorne stehen. Die erste Frage sollte nie lauten: Welches Tool nehmen wir? Sie sollte lauten: Was sollen die Schüler*innen lernen, und wie können digitale Medien sie dabei unterstützen? Das klingt banal, wird im Alltag aber oft umgekehrt gemacht.

Dazu kommt Zeit. Kollegien brauchen Raum, um Neues auszuprobieren und sich auszutauschen. Schon eine einzelne Fortbildung kann manchmal einiges anstoßen. Nachhaltig wird es aber dann, wenn eine Schule ein gemeinsames Zielbild hat und Schritt für Schritt daran arbeitet.

Lehrkräfte sollten dabei keine Systemadministratoren sein müssen. Wenn das WLAN streikt oder die Geräte nicht synchronisieren, kostet das Unterrichtszeit und Nerven. Ein verlässlicher Support durch einen starken IT-Partner ist deshalb auch eine pädagogische Frage.

**Gerade künstliche Intelligenz verunsichert viele Lehrkräfte. Was brauchen sie?**

Vor allem Orientierung. Das merken wir auch an den Anfragen: Kaum ein Fortbildungsthema ist bei uns derzeit so gefragt wie KI. Viele Lehrkräfte haben KI schon ausprobiert, oft privat und ohne klaren Rahmen. In der Schule kommen Fragen zum Datenschutz, zur Leistungsbewertung und zur eigenen Rolle dazu. In unseren Fortbildungen geht es deshalb nicht nur um einzelne Anwendungen, sondern auch um eine Haltung: Wo entlastet mich KI wirklich, etwa bei der Vorbereitung oder bei der Differenzierung? Und wo muss ich genau hinschauen? Am meisten profitieren die Schüler*innen, wenn ihre Lehrkräfte sicher mit KI umgehen.

**Eingangs haben Sie gesagt, Schulen sollten jetzt wissen, wo sie stehen. Dafür hat Converge Germany einen Readiness Check Digitalpakt 2.0 entwickelt. Was steckt dahinter?**

Der Check ist eine Standortbestimmung für Schulen und Schulträger. Er umfasst 18 Fragen zu Infrastruktur und Ausstattung, zum digitalen Lernen und Lehren, zu Personal und Kompetenzen, zu Recht, Sicherheit und Datenschutz sowie zu Strategie, Budget und Teilhabe. Das Ausfüllen dauert nur etwa acht Minuten und ist kostenlos. Danach gibt es per E-Mail zu jedem Bereich eine Einschätzung und konkrete Empfehlungen.

title: Eine Hürde weniger für Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin
subtitle: Vanessa Emde ist raus aus der Berliner Linksfraktion - und auf dem Weg zu Rot-Grün-Rot haben Linke, Grüne und SPD ein Problem weniger.
feedText: Vanessa Emde ist raus aus der Berliner Linksfraktion - und auf dem Weg zu Rot-Grün-Rot haben Linke, Grüne und SPD ein Problem weniger. Das letzte wird es wohl nicht bleiben. Vanessa Emde wurde aus ihrer Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Sie war wegen ihrer Haltung zu Israel unter Druck geraten. Für die Regierungsbildung in Berlin ist es ein wichtiger Schritt. Vor Raum 311 im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus herrscht ein gewaltiger Medienrummel.
articleBody:
# Linke schliesst Emde aus: Eine Hürde weniger für Rot-Grün-Rot

## Linkenfraktion schliesst Vanessa Emde aus : Eine Hürde weniger für Rot-Grün-Rot

von Markus Gross

Vanessa Emde ist raus aus der Berliner Linksfraktion - und auf dem Weg zu Rot-Grün-Rot haben Linke, Grüne und SPD ein Problem weniger. Das letzte wird es wohl nicht bleiben.

Vanessa Emde wurde aus ihrer Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Sie war wegen ihrer Haltung zu Israel unter Druck geraten. Für die Regierungsbildung in Berlin ist es ein wichtiger Schritt.

Vor Raum 311 im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus herrscht ein gewaltiger Medienrummel. Drinnen im großen Sitzungssaal diskutiert die Linksfraktion lebhaft über den Ausschluss von Vanessa Emde. Es scheint, als würde die halbe Republik auf ein Zeichen warten. Schafft es die Fraktionsführung, die aus ihrer Sicht widerspenstige Abgeordnete rauszuschmeißen?

Nach zweieinhalb Stunden steht fest: Vanessa Emde ist nicht mehr Mitglied der Fraktion Die Linke . 33 Abgeordnete stimmen für ihren Ausschluss, sechs stimmen mit Nein, es gibt vier Enthaltungen. Die nötige Mehrheit von 30 Stimmen wird erreicht.

- Umstrittene Abgeordnete: Vanessa Emde aus Berliner Linken-Fraktion ausgeschlossen
Sichtlich angespannt verkündet der Fraktionschef der Linken, Tobias Schulz: "Wir haben keine Möglichkeit mehr gesehen, mit Frau Emde weiter zusammenzuarbeiten." Sie habe sich nicht an Partei- und Fraktionsbeschlüsse zum Thema Antisemitismus gehalten. "Ihr Ausschluss ist folgerichtig", so Schulz weiter.

ZDF-Korrespondent Stephan Merseburger ordnet aus Berlin den Fraktionsausschluss Vanessa Emdes ein.

## Unterstützer empfangen Emde mit Jubel

Als Vanessa Emde den Fraktionssaal verlässt, wartet schon ein zwölfköpfiges Unterstützerkomitee auf sie. Es gibt Jubelrufe, als sie erscheint, Umarmungen und Zeichen der Solidarität. Emde bezeichnete ihren Ausschluss in einem Statement als Ergebnis einer "medialen Hetzkampagne".

Ihre Fraktion habe offenbar dem Druck von SPD und Grünen nachgegeben. Sie wolle ihr Mandat behalten. Ihre Unterstützer ruft sie dazu auf, sich zu "organisieren". Kämpferisch ihr Schlusswort:

> Wir sehen uns im Kiez und wir sehen uns am Streikposten! In diesem Sinne: Yalla, yalla, Klassenkampf, Freiheit für Palästina! „

Vanessa Emde

## Grüne und SPD sehen positives Signal

Die möglichen Koalitionspartner SPD und Grüne begrüßten den Ausschluss von Vanessa Emde. Werner Graf, Co-Chef der Grünenfraktion, gab sich zufrieden: "Die Entscheidung zeigt, dass für israelbezogenen Antisemitismus in einer rot-grün-roten Regierung kein Platz ist" . Steffen Krach, Co-Chef der SPD-Fraktion, der zuvor vehement einen Ausschluss Emdes gefordert hatte, ergänzte:

> Die Entscheidung der Linksfraktion ist eine gute Nachricht für die weiteren Koalitionsverhandlungen. „

Steffen Krach, Co-Chef der Berliner SPD-Fraktion

Die Berliner Linke hat die Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde aus ihrer Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Den Schritt hat man sich laut dem Fraktionsvorsitzenden Schulze nicht leicht gemacht.

## Antisemitismus-Vorwürfe gegen Emde

Vanessa Emde, mit über 46 Prozent direkt gewählte Abgeordnete in Neukölln, hatte zuvor mit ihren israelkritischen Aussagen immer wieder für Diskussionen gesorgt. Zuletzt hatte Emde in einem Instagram-Post das Existenzrecht Israels als jüdischer Staat angezweifelt. Ihre Kritiker werteten das als antisemitisch.

Der Zentralrat der Juden zeigte sich tief besorgt und forderte die Linke zum Handeln auf. Auch SPD und Grüne, die möglichen Koalitionspartner, waren verstimmt und machten den Ausschluss Emdes zur Bedingung.

- Schuster: Ausschluss von Emde "nur ein erster Schritt"
Bei den Grünen schaltete sich zuletzt sogar die Bundespitze ein. "Wenn das scheitert, kann ich allen nur abraten, in eine Regierung mit einer politischen Führung zu gehen, die in der eigenen Fraktion keine Macht hat" , hatte die Grünen-Co-Vorsitzende Franziska Brantner noch der "Frankfurter Allgemeinen Zeitung" vom Dienstag gesagt.

Die Berliner Linke hat die Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde aus der Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Was bedeutet die Entscheidung für die Partei und die Regierungsbildung in Berlin? ZDFheute live analysiert.

## Misstrauen bei SPD und Grünen bleibt

Mit dem Ausschluss Vanessa Emdes ist eine der größten Hürden auf dem Weg zu Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin aus dem Weg geräumt. Doch Entwarnung bedeutet das nicht. SPD und Grüne bleiben misstrauisch. Der Vorwurf, in Teilen der Linken gebe es ein strukturelles Problem mit antisemitischen Tendenzen, ist längst nicht ausgeräumt.

Auch innerparteilich ist der Konflikt keineswegs beendet. Sechs Gegenstimmen und vier Enthaltungen zeigen, dass Emde weiterhin Rückhalt in der Fraktion hat. Wie sich ihr Unterstützerlager künftig positioniert, dürfte für die Koalitionsgespräche entscheidend werden. Der Politikwissenschaftler Thorsten Faas findet: "Der Ausschluss ist nicht so überzeugend, dass jegliche Diskussion innerhalb der Linken beendet ist." Das Bündnis bleibe in einem Schwebezustand.

Vorerst aber können alle Beteiligten aufatmen: Die Gespräche gehen weiter. Bis zum Jahreswechsel soll ein Koalitionsvertrag stehen. Anschließend müssen Linke und SPD noch ihre Mitglieder überzeugen. Doch bis dahin ist es ein weiter Weg - und das nächste Personalproblem womöglich nur eine Frage der Zeit.

Markus Gross ist Redakteur im ZDF-Landesstudio Berlin.

Lassen Sie sich Beiträge von ZDFheute bevorzugt bei Google anzeigen

ZDF-Korrespondent Stephan Merseburger ordnet aus Berlin den Fraktionsausschluss Vanessa Emdes ein.

## Unterstützer empfangen Emde mit Jubel

Als Vanessa Emde den Fraktionssaal verlässt, wartet schon ein zwölfköpfiges Unterstützerkomitee auf sie. Es gibt Jubelrufe, als sie erscheint, Umarmungen und Zeichen der Solidarität. Emde bezeichnete ihren Ausschluss in einem Statement als Ergebnis einer "medialen Hetzkampagne".

Ihre Fraktion habe offenbar dem Druck von SPD und Grünen nachgegeben. Sie wolle ihr Mandat behalten. Ihre Unterstützer ruft sie dazu auf, sich zu "organisieren". Kämpferisch ihr Schlusswort:

> Wir sehen uns im Kiez und wir sehen uns am Streikposten! In diesem Sinne: Yalla, yalla, Klassenkampf, Freiheit für Palästina! „

Vanessa Emde

## Grüne und SPD sehen positives Signal

Die möglichen Koalitionspartner SPD und Grüne begrüßten den Ausschluss von Vanessa Emde. Werner Graf, Co-Chef der Grünenfraktion, gab sich zufrieden: "Die Entscheidung zeigt, dass für israelbezogenen Antisemitismus in einer rot-grün-roten Regierung kein Platz ist" . Steffen Krach, Co-Chef der SPD-Fraktion, der zuvor vehement einen Ausschluss Emdes gefordert hatte, ergänzte:

> Die Entscheidung der Linksfraktion ist eine gute Nachricht für die weiteren Koalitionsverhandlungen. „

Steffen Krach, Co-Chef der Berliner SPD-Fraktion

Die Berliner Linke hat die Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde aus ihrer Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Den Schritt hat man sich laut dem Fraktionsvorsitzenden Schulze nicht leicht gemacht.

## Antisemitismus-Vorwürfe gegen Emde

Vanessa Emde, mit über 46 Prozent direkt gewählte Abgeordnete in Neukölln, hatte zuvor mit ihren israelkritischen Aussagen immer wieder für Diskussionen gesorgt. Zuletzt hatte Emde in einem Instagram-Post das Existenzrecht Israels als jüdischer Staat angezweifelt. Ihre Kritiker werteten das als antisemitisch.

Der Zentralrat der Juden zeigte sich tief besorgt und forderte die Linke zum Handeln auf. Auch SPD und Grüne, die möglichen Koalitionspartner, waren verstimmt und machten den Ausschluss Emdes zur Bedingung.

- Schuster: Ausschluss von Emde "nur ein erster Schritt"
Bei den Grünen schaltete sich zuletzt sogar die Bundespitze ein. "Wenn das scheitert, kann ich allen nur abraten, in eine Regierung mit einer politischen Führung zu gehen, die in der eigenen Fraktion keine Macht hat" , hatte die Grünen-Co-Vorsitzende Franziska Brantner noch der "Frankfurter Allgemeinen Zeitung" vom Dienstag gesagt.

Die Berliner Linke hat die Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde aus der Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Was bedeutet die Entscheidung für die Partei und die Regierungsbildung in Berlin? ZDFheute live analysiert.

## Misstrauen bei SPD und Grünen bleibt

Mit dem Ausschluss Vanessa Emdes ist eine der größten Hürden auf dem Weg zu Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin aus dem Weg geräumt. Doch Entwarnung bedeutet das nicht. SPD und Grüne bleiben misstrauisch. Der Vorwurf, in Teilen der Linken gebe es ein strukturelles Problem mit antisemitischen Tendenzen, ist längst nicht ausgeräumt.

Auch innerparteilich ist der Konflikt keineswegs beendet. Sechs Gegenstimmen und vier Enthaltungen zeigen, dass Emde weiterhin Rückhalt in der Fraktion hat. Wie sich ihr Unterstützerlager künftig positioniert, dürfte für die Koalitionsgespräche entscheidend werden. Der Politikwissenschaftler Thorsten Faas findet: "Der Ausschluss ist nicht so überzeugend, dass jegliche Diskussion innerhalb der Linken beendet ist." Das Bündnis bleibe in einem Schwebezustand.

Vorerst aber können alle Beteiligten aufatmen: Die Gespräche gehen weiter. Bis zum Jahreswechsel soll ein Koalitionsvertrag stehen. Anschließend müssen Linke und SPD noch ihre Mitglieder überzeugen. Doch bis dahin ist es ein weiter Weg - und das nächste Personalproblem womöglich nur eine Frage der Zeit.

Markus Gross ist Redakteur im ZDF-Landesstudio Berlin.

title: Dezeen reports from New York's new November design week
subtitle: A collection of showcases, old and new, took place in New York this November, effectively adding a second design week to a city already loaded with…
feedText: Dezeen's US editor Ben Dreith explores the offerings. The as-yet-unofficial design week in the first weeks of November came into focus earlier this year, when trade fair ICFF, anchor fair of NYCxDesign, announced that in 2027 it will take place simultaneously with sister fair BDNY, which has been held in November for years. articleBody:
A collection of showcases, old and new, took place in [New York](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/new-york-city/) this November, effectively adding a second design week to a city already loaded with events. Dezeen's US editor Ben Dreith explores the offerings.

The as-yet-unofficial design week in the first weeks of November came into focus earlier this year, when trade fair ICFF, anchor fair of [NYCxDesign](https://nycxdesign.org/), [announced that in 2027 it will take place simultaneously](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/05/12/icff-new-york-november-2027/) with sister fair BDNY, which has been held in November for years.

The move has prompted questions in the city about the future of the NYCxDesign festival in May and what a November design week would look like.

Dudd Haus at Collectible design fair was a standout booth from the week. Photo by Matthew Gordon

While BDNY and high-end showcase [Salon Art + Design](https://www.thesalonny.com/) have always been held in November, other design fairs have sprouted to take advantage of the opportunity to show during this busy period.

The week is positioning itself, without any explicit organisation, as a massive event in the New York design calendar.

Even NYCxDesign, still scheduled for May as usual in 2027, held a November event bringing in designers [Ross Lovegrove](https://www.rosslovegrove.com/), [Karim Rashid](https://www.karimrashid.com/) and [Rem D Koolhaas](https://www.instagram.com/rem_un/?hl=en) for a talk moderated by New York-based design writer [Camille Okhio](https://camilleokhio.com/).

The panellists spoke about the potential for AI and derided the inclusion of craft in conversations about design. However, as writer Debika Ray noted in an opinion piece for Dezeen, [crafted, one-off pieces have lately come to dominate design shows](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/09/16/how-craft-conquered-design/).

NYCxDesign staking out a talk with well-known industrial designers suggests that its May event could be devoted to industrial design, while November complements it with a focus on collectible furniture.

This was definitely true this year, when collectible designs dominated the November showcases.

A screen by Wiktoria & Filip Bielicki at Objekt Gallery's Collectible booth showcased a trend towards reliefs during the design week. Photo by Simon Leung

Among these was the Brussels-founded design fair [Collectible](https://collectible.design/). For its third New York iteration, it moved from office tower-turned creative hub WSA to a defunct movie theatre on the Upper East Side that is being developed by entities [related to WSA](https://therealdeal.com/new-york/2026/09/22/stellbergers-happier-grocery-heads-to-upper-east-side/).

While the unfinished theatre fit the experimental nature of the work, the execution was, by some accounts, chaotic, with one worker being sent to the hospital after an unstable light fell onto her head.

Collectible called it an "isolated occurrence involving an exhibitor's equipment".

"The safety of our exhibitors, staff and visitors is a priority, and we take any reported incident seriously," a representative for Collectible told Dezeen.

"Collectible maintains safety procedures for the fair and expects all exhibitors to ensure that their own equipment is installed and secured appropriately."

[Read: Eighteen weird, wonderful and well-made objects from NYCxDesign 2026](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/05/27/eighteen-objects-nycxdesign-2026/)

Despite some chaos, including recently laid cement, there were strong showings. Philadelphia-based [Dudd Haus](https://www.duddhaus.com/?srsltid=AYCX9vIyaH2V17-zeh1tz7VhlvjqLSL2DcCwQCyXkGEAr9oH6VCMhiHC) showed a pared-down booth with its usual mix of conceptual one-offs. Particularly of note was a milled-aluminium floor lamp by [Jordan Maurice](https://www.instagram.com/jordan__maurice/?hl=en) and a paravent made with telephone cords by [Overt Cove](https://www.overtcove.com/).

Also eye-catching was a booth of droopy glass lamps and shades with erotic overtones by [Upstate New York gallery Freaks](https://freaksny.com/), and another sensual booth with drapes and lacquered furniture by [Iitem studio](https://iitem.nyc/).

The fair's scenography carried the sleek, modern, USM-laden feel from the prior additions. Curators [Alex Tieghi-Walker](https://alextiwa.com/) and [Lynette Nylander](https://www.instagram.com/lynettesaid/?hl=en) designed special sections.

Bas-reliefs were popular on otherwise modern furniture, including a battened screen by Polish studio [Wiktoria & Filip Bielicki](https://www.instagram.com/wiktoria.and.filip/) for [Objekt Gallery](https://objekt.gallery/) and a coffee table with raised ceramic on its base by [Small Things Studio](https://www.smallthingsstudios.com/) for [Salon 21](https://www.salontwenty-one.com/).

Montreal collective Ensemble took over Yabu Pushelberg's New York office, creating a plywood gallery within the office. Photo by Simon S Belleau

At Collectible, [Montreal design collective Ensemble](https://www.instagram.com/ensssemble/) showcased its members' work on nooks in a wall made with USM panels.

This was just a taste of what Ensemble had in store for the week. The collective brought their signature experimentation to [Yabu Pushelberg](https://www.yabupushelberg.com/)’s Tribeca studio, creating a plywood room-within-a-room to showcase work, including new lamps by [Zebulon Perron](https://zebulonperron.com/), sculptural glass lamps by [Alex Joncas](https://alexjoncas.com/), metal works by [Jérémy Paguet](https://studiopaguet.com/), leather lamps by [Jeta Studio](https://www.jeta.studio/en) and brass-lined mirrors by [Jeremy Le Chatelier](https://www.jeremylechatelier.com/).

It was an extremely focused showing that proved sometimes you can do more with less.

Zarolat showed a light by Natural Urbano and Polybion at Salon Art + Design. Photo by Peter Baker

At Salon Art + Design, a few younger galleries stuck out from the historical work and ultra-high-end designs that usually characterise the fair.

Brooklyn-based [Zarolat’](https://www.zarolat.com/)s showing included ash-wood lamps with cellulose shades by Natural Urbano and [Polybion](https://www.polybion.bio/stories/lapso-lamp-celium-natural-urbano/), while New York-based hub for Brazilian furniture, [Bossa Furniture,](https://www.bossafurniture.com/) showcased a greatest hits of mid-century São Paulo makers, including Joaquim Tenreiro.

Marquel Williams showcased his eye for curation at Basic Space. Photo by Alexa Bendek

BDNY was, as usual, where most of the actual commerce took place during the week. While the interior designers and architects descended on the sample-forward showing, a few brands showed stand-out collections, including [Sancal](https://sancal.com/en/)’s showing of [Júlia Esqué](https://www.juliaesque.com/)’s playfully fringed armchairs and [Santa & Cole](https://www.google.com/aclk?sa=L&pf=1&ai=DChsSEwje7fOMgp-YAxUHNggFHZ7aCU0YACICCAEQShoCbWQ&co=1&ase=2&gclid=CjwKCAiA5Y_YBhBbEiwAK5Dl7cedY5pBcw4_HEyPPJe5cJc7Rz1AMwGwaNpm-E8szWuR_-fZUsOJXxoCAK0QAvD_BwE&cid=CAASZeRoDA2NIOezVp_FsM14SYphXNqo9iK8oXfq-F6AiBvDQec27YQA0PRzI6GaWopWTuNDxN4r8ZeU8WwVwAet0mr-gGVjYwn_dOtyytpaII0us7GHLq-rbbcVRUyc5lPqEZRXV_7g&cce=2&category=acrcp_v1_32&sig=AOD64_2zLBRippXaofpKzhQMv1AN0uVwQA&q&nis=4&adurl=https://www.lumens.com/santa-and-cole/?utm_source%3Dgoogle%26utm_medium%3DPLA%26utm_campaign%3D20317852977%26gad_source%3D1%26gad_campaignid%3D20322734537%26gbraid%3D0AAAAADo8bk00cW596HcniKPQQLlttXBRN%26gclid%3DCjwKCAiA5Y_YBhBbEiwAK5Dl7cedY5pBcw4_HEyPPJe5cJc7Rz1AMwGwaNpm-E8szWuR_-fZUsOJXxoCAK0QAvD_BwE&ved=2ahUKEwi_6e2Mgp-YAxW_v4kEHegfLBMQ0Qx6BAguEAE)’s modern, fun lighting.

Later in the week, LA-based [Basic Space](https://basic.space/?srsltid=AYCX9vLG1NPJWwKXeEjPNNB-H77p3OaYOEOuiXqmTAgUDTVeWZgtXkEN), run by the organisers behind Design Miami, returned to SoHo. With artistic direction by [Alexander May](https://www.instagram.com/alexander____may/?hl=en), the stark, white-cube approach differed from the in-situ, multi-room afair that characterised the first New York Basic Space in 2025.

Harry Nuriev showcased a metallic installation informed by airline seats. Photo by Alexa Bendek

The fair featured a focus on big names and multiple co-curators competing for attention on the promotional materials and in the execution.

Standout pieces included the live-edge wood furniture with small metal connective elements by Brooklyn-based designer [Gregory Beson](https://gregorybeson.com/), as well as [Daniel Swarilov](https://swarilov.com/)’s metal credenzas, in a section curated by [Marquel Williams](https://marquelwilliams.com/).

Paris-based [Harry Nuriev](https://crosbystudios.com/) created a metallic take on first-class airline seats as a standalone installation. Another booth featured an oversized sofa by NFL player Stefon Diggs' luxury furniture brand Si Vis Pacem, illustrating the fair's mix of design with celebrity culture.

Fábrica brought its "travelling living room" to New York. Photo by Darryl Richardson

Finally, Mexico City-based creative studio Fábrica, run by artist [Darryl Richardson](https://www.darryl-richardson.com/info) and partner [Maryah Ananda](https://www.maryahananda.com/), held its La Sala showcase in a loft near Penn Station.

With a focus on international Black designers, the showcase featured art and design, with the space shaped like a living room by interior designer [Johnathan Bailey](https://www.instagram.com/johnbaileyy/?hl=en).

Furniture pieces of note included a slim metal chair by [Kai Avent-deLeo](https://www.instagram.com/kaiaventdeleon/?hl=en) and an armchair by [Mark Grattan](https://markgrattan.com/).

The social focus of the event gave it an aesthetic heft, and a few of its stated goals, “community over curation” and “warmth over spectacle”, made it stand out from many of the other offerings from the week.

Judging by the willingness of the different fall fairs to join in, it seems likely that the November design week will fully take off.

articleBody:
# Tech Giants Are Effectively Ungovernable. Here’s How to Change That.

## Tech Giants Are Effectively Ungovernable. Here’s How to Change That.

## The return of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang exposes a dangerous gap in corporate oversight.

American business has minted a new brand of executive: the CEO who is too big to fire. On Nov. 17, Nvidia’s board declared that it had accepted the resignation of Jensen Huang, felled by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and a romance with one of the executive’s own subordinates. Six days later, Huang was back, restored after a unanimous vote by the same board. Nvidia’s shares soared. Many investors celebrated the return of the leather-jacketed founder credited with making the company the engine of the artificial intelligence revolution.

Three years earlier, OpenAI’s board had dismissed Sam Altman, citing a lack of candor with directors. Five days later, Altman returned, and most of the directors responsible for his removal were out.

American business has minted a new brand of executive: the CEO who is too big to fire. On Nov. 17, Nvidia’s board declared that it had accepted the resignation of Jensen Huang, felled by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and a romance with one of the executive’s own subordinates. Six days later, Huang was back, restored after a unanimous vote by the same board. Nvidia’s shares soared. Many investors celebrated the return of the leather-jacketed founder credited with making the company the engine of the artificial intelligence revolution.

Three years earlier, OpenAI’s board had dismissed Sam Altman, citing a lack of candor with directors. Five days later, Altman returned, and most of the directors responsible for his removal were out.

In both cases, directors discovered that formal authority to remove a chief executive does not mean the power to do so in practice. The episodes exposed a three-pronged weakness in corporate governance: the challenge of maverick founders, the extraordinary complexity of AI, and the growing dependence of the U.S. economy and national security on a handful of companies at the technological frontier.

Both Altman and Huang have personas, know-how, and market-moving power that made them unfireable. Yet if the boards of the country’s most consequential technology firms cannot exercise ultimate authority over management, these companies are effectively ungovernable. This reveals a major gap in corporate stewardship, underscoring the imperative of robust regulation to ensure that the vulnerabilities of powerful U.S. companies do not become fatal weaknesses for the country’s democracy and society writ large.

The iconic corporate founder is a hallmark of U.S. business culture. Henry Ford and Andrew Carnegie shaped society-altering industries around their personalities and distinctive working styles. Steve Jobs provides the most celebrated historic example of this type of figure in tech. Forced out of Apple in 1985, Jobs returned in 1997 when the company was in steep decline. His track record of inventiveness helped win back employees, customers, investors, and developers. He also persuaded Bill Gates to invest $150 million in Apple and commit to developing Microsoft software for Macintosh computers, building an ecosystem whose fortunes were intertwined with his own and that has dominated the market for decades.

These bold founders may have as much in common with an artist or creator than they do with fellow CEOs. A great architect or film director works with large teams but puts an unmistakable stamp on their work. Although a studio or tradition can continue after its originator dies or departs, investors, collaborators, and audiences do not always stay on.

This analogy helps explain why succession at frontier technology companies is so fraught. Investors bet on a founder’s judgment about technologies whose commercial potential is unproven. Engineers are inspired by a particular visionary. Customers and business partners invest in the future that the founder promises. As these forces rally, they reify perceptions of an individual’s genius, which attracts still more talent and capital. Confidence becomes self-perpetuating.

Such devotion is measurable. Huang topped Glassdoor’s 2026 ranking of CEOs with a 99 percent approval rating among employee reviewers. Thousands of employees reportedly signed a letter seeking his reinstatement this month. His reportedly cruel behavior toward certain employees seemingly did little to puncture that aura.

OpenAI’s 2023 crisis demonstrated the power of such fealty. After its board fired Altman, more than 95 percent of the company’s employees signed a letter threatening to resign unless he came back. Microsoft, OpenAI’s largest commercial partner, rolled out a red carpet to Altman, promising to allow him to rebuild his team there. Faced with losing the workforce that was OpenAI’s principal asset, the board folded. The employees, investors, and commercial partners whose confidence had helped make Altman successful overpowered those charged with supervising him.

These examples do not prove that founders are irreplaceable. Apple’s revenues more than doubled during the early years of John Sculley’s post-Jobs tenure in the 1980s; more recently, the company has thrived under Tim Cook since Jobs’s death. When Uber’s Travis Kalanick was forced out in 2017, investors worried about losing the transportation innovator’s aggressive founder. His successor, Dara Khosrowshahi, now presides over a company that generated $193 billion in gross bookings and $10 billion in free cash flow in 2025.

Board members are a little like grandparents. They admire and care about the baby, comforted that the parent—the CEO—does the daily grind. When the parent disappears, the board is left holding a crying, demanding infant. Sedate quarterly meetings suddenly turn into frantic round-the-clock Zooms. Having lost the one person who they trusted to raise the child, boards want nothing more than to once again pass the progeny into capable hands.

When it comes to AI companies, the problem is magnified by the extraordinary gap between a CEO’s knowledge of frontier technologies and what even accomplished directors can understand. Nvidia’s 10-person board includes Melissa Lora, the former president of Taco Bell; Stephen Neal, a distinguished trial lawyer; and Dawn Hudson, a former Pepsi-Cola and National Football League marketing executive. Three of the 10 have served on the board for more than 28 years each. Just one is under the age of 60. While several board members have technology backgrounds, the emergence of Nvidia’s chips and financing as lynchpins of AI competition has transformed the demands on a group of directors who were chosen at least in part because Huang trusted them not to get in his way . Alongside bleeding-edge technologies, the board is now dealing with matters of foreign espionage, regulatory capture, securities fraud, and export controls. It’s not hard to imagine Nvidia’s directors feeling out of their depth.

The governance challenges created by Nvidia’s technological complexity are compounded by the company’s centrality to the U.S. economy and national security. A 2026 investment analysis estimated that 42 AI-related stocks accounted for 60 percent of the S&P 500’s gains in 2025. By September 2026, Nvidia alone represented approximately 8.4 percent of the index. Huang’s reinstatement on Monday propelled a broader market rally, underscoring how closely U.S. financial fortunes have become tied to confidence in the AI industry. The national-security dependence is at least as consequential. AI is increasingly incorporated into military intelligence, surveillance, cyber operations, logistics, and command-and-control systems. Access to advanced computing is at the heart of competitive tensions with China.

These dependencies help explain U.S. President Donald Trump’s extraordinary intervention in Nvidia’s leadership deliberations. According to Semafor , the president called into a Nvidia board meeting to press for Huang’s return, suggesting that China might recruit him if Nvidia failed to take him back. Though no investigation has been completed and the allegations of Chinese plotting to compromise Huang are alarming , Trump personally vouched that his return would pose no national security risk. It is hard to know who possesses greater leverage in the Trump-Huang relationship—the president who controls regulatory decisions or the corporate titan whose technology is essential to domestic prosperity and national security.

Reliance on individual technology entrepreneurs for vital national functions can compromise public interests. In October, Ukrainian forces experienced serious disruptions to Starshield satellite communications, impairing military operations. Elon Musk subsequently acknowledged that his company, SpaceX, had restricted certain uses of the service, though responsibility for the disruptions remains contested. Society depends on interconnected technological systems that are vulnerable to malfunction and compromise; the power vested in a handful of tech moguls who control these networks is staggering.

U.S. institutions have failed to reckon with this amalgamation of power. Congress remains divided over how to regulate AI. Federal agencies possess fragmented authority over specific risks and no mandate from the White House to address them. Companies develop capabilities faster than public institutions can assess them. CEOs with immense technical resources and public influence end up guiding the officials responsible for overseeing them.

U.S. corporate leadership is predicated on the perception that U.S. companies operate within a system of enforceable laws, strong oversight, and credible government institutions. But if U.S. boards cannot meaningfully restrain powerful executives, and the president can intervene in their internal deliberations, those differentiators collapse. The obvious response is to strengthen corporate oversight. Some mechanisms already exist. Nvidia has an independent board, audit and governance committees, and a confidential reporting hotline. It has now added a specialized national security committee and is upgrading its compliance function. OpenAI maintains a safety and security committee overseeing its operations. But all these arrangements depend on directors whose authority may be subsumed by founder loyalty, commercial pressure, and technological complexity.

Other highly regulated industries offer more robust, proven oversight models. Under Federal Reserve rules, large bank holding companies must maintain independent risk committees, including directors with relevant expertise; chief risk officers report directly to those committees as well as management. Britain requires senior executives at financial firms to be approved by regulators, makes it clear what each is responsible for, and can hold them personally accountable if they fail to take reasonable steps to prevent wrongdoing. U.S. pharmaceutical regulation provides another precedent. Federal rules give drug manufacturers’ quality-control arms the authority to approve or reject products and manufacturing procedures, so that decisions do not lie simply with a CEO’s commercial preferences.

These models suggest an approach to governing companies whose technologies pose exceptional public risks. Congress should establish an independent federal supervisory authority for designated frontier AI companies, including critical infrastructure providers and developers of exceptionally capable models. Its jurisdiction should depend on the risks and systemic importance of technology companies, rather than their size or public-company status. Now that corporate interests have captured the U.S. executive branch, legislative oversight is essential.

Such an institution would need permanent technical staff with expertise in advanced computing, model capabilities, cybersecurity, and intelligence threats. It would require secure access to proprietary information, the power to inspect governance systems, and the authority to compel corrective action. Its independence from day-to-day political intervention would be essential.

Meanwhile, regulated companies should have dedicated board-level risk committees staffed by directors with technical and national-security competence. Those committees should retain their own expert advisors and receive regular reports from both the CEO and independent risk, safety, and compliance officers. Boards should be required to document how they evaluate consequential decisions, oversee potential conflicts of interest, and prepare for abrupt leadership transitions.

A further priority is genuine protection for whistleblowers. Nvidia’s formal policies prohibit retaliation, yet recent reporting suggests that employees fear speaking openly. In technology companies, confidentiality is increasingly difficult to preserve. Employers can potentially reconstruct a source’s identity from records of device use, badge access, communications, and document activity, even when a reporter or investigator promises anonymity. One shudders to think what this might mean for Nvidia employees who recently spoke out about mistreatment or alleged misdeeds, believing that Huang’s tenure was over for good.

A modern whistleblower regime should offer secure channels outside the company, enforceable restrictions on attempts to identify confidential sources, and meaningful penalties for retaliation. An independent regulator should interview employees and business partners without requiring them to expose themselves to management. Such protections are particularly important during investigations involving a powerful founder.

It may be tempting to conclude that Nvidia’s crisis ended happily once Huang returned and the market rallied. The OpenAI episode invited a similar reaction, especially as the company continued its rapid expansion after Altman’s reinstatement. But neither recovery resolves the institutional weakness that allowed directors’ decisions to be reversed under pressure.

U.S. technological leadership cannot depend on a system in which the most influential executives are effectively irreplaceable. A company that is too big to lose its founder may also be too powerful to govern itself. As AI becomes embedded in the economy, national security, and public life, the United States needs oversight institutions capable of withstanding the demands of employees, investors, politicians, and even the most celebrated innovators. The long-term credibility of U.S. technological leadership will depend on it.

articleBody:
# Preisrutsch: Butter kostet wieder weniger als ein Euro

Gerade jetzt in der Vorweihnachtszeit greifen viele Menschen großzügiger bei der Butter zu. Denn sie wird für zahlreiche Plätzchenrezepte gebraucht. Da wird diese Nachricht einige Verbraucher freuen: Butter wird in Deutschland wieder günstiger. Wie die Discounter Aldi und Lidl mitteilten, kostet eine 250-Gramm-Packung Deutsche Markenbutter der Eigenmarken ab Mittwoch (25. November) nur noch 99 Cent nach zuletzt 1,15 Euro.

- Zum Artikel: Milchpreis unter Druck – Warum Bauern in München protestieren
## Andere Händler ziehen häufig nach

Als Grund für die Preissenkungen nannte Aldi gesunkene Einkaufspreise. Die Preise für Butter hätten sich in den vergangenen Wochen entlang der Lieferkette rückläufig entwickelt. Die Preisvorteile gebe das Unternehmen nun an seine Kunden weiter. Lidl führte die Preissenkung auf gesunkene Rohstoffpreise zurück.

Wenn in der Vergangenheit einzelne Lebensmittelhändler sogenannte Eckpreisartikel wie Butter dauerhaft reduzierten, folgten andere Handelsketten üblicherweise schnell.

## Butterpreise schwanken stark

Der Butterpreis schwankt seit einiger Zeit stark, abhängig von Milchmengen und Nachfrage. Im Oktober 2024 wurde der bislang höchste Stand erreicht: 2,39 Euro für das günstigste Päckchen der Eigenmarken. Schon ein gutes Jahr später rutschte der Preis schon einmal unter einen Euro .

Damals zeigte sich der Bayerische Bauernverband alarmiert, der Preisverfall sei verantwortungslos. Bei einem Verbraucherpreis von 0,99 Euro seien die Produktionskosten in der Lebensmittelkette nicht gedeckt – weder bei den Molkereien noch bei den Landwirten, argumentierte der Verband.

Das ist die Europäische Perspektive bei BR24.

# Preisrutsch: Butter kostet wieder weniger als ein Euro

Gerade jetzt in der Vorweihnachtszeit greifen viele Menschen großzügiger bei der Butter zu. Denn sie wird für zahlreiche Plätzchenrezepte gebraucht. Da wird diese Nachricht einige Verbraucher freuen: Butter wird in Deutschland wieder günstiger. Wie die Discounter Aldi und Lidl mitteilten, kostet eine 250-Gramm-Packung Deutsche Markenbutter der Eigenmarken ab Mittwoch (25. November) nur noch 99 Cent nach zuletzt 1,15 Euro.

- Zum Artikel: Milchpreis unter Druck – Warum Bauern in München protestieren
## Andere Händler ziehen häufig nach

Als Grund für die Preissenkungen nannte Aldi gesunkene Einkaufspreise. Die Preise für Butter hätten sich in den vergangenen Wochen entlang der Lieferkette rückläufig entwickelt. Die Preisvorteile gebe das Unternehmen nun an seine Kunden weiter. Lidl führte die Preissenkung auf gesunkene Rohstoffpreise zurück.

Wenn in der Vergangenheit einzelne Lebensmittelhändler sogenannte Eckpreisartikel wie Butter dauerhaft reduzierten, folgten andere Handelsketten üblicherweise schnell.

## Butterpreise schwanken stark

Der Butterpreis schwankt seit einiger Zeit stark, abhängig von Milchmengen und Nachfrage. Im Oktober 2024 wurde der bislang höchste Stand erreicht: 2,39 Euro für das günstigste Päckchen der Eigenmarken. Schon ein gutes Jahr später rutschte der Preis schon einmal unter einen Euro .

Damals zeigte sich der Bayerische Bauernverband alarmiert, der Preisverfall sei verantwortungslos. Bei einem Verbraucherpreis von 0,99 Euro seien die Produktionskosten in der Lebensmittelkette nicht gedeckt – weder bei den Molkereien noch bei den Landwirten, argumentierte der Verband.

Das ist die Europäische Perspektive bei BR24.

articleBody:
# What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?

Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis . The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

It’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

## Tackling Riemann

The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, “It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field.”

The proof of the hypothesis was announced by a mathematician named Levent Alpöge, who has been working at Anthropic, and, not surprisingly, used Claude to generate it. His announcement is written in a somewhat florid style (example: “one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph”), and he has apparently dropped some hints that some of it was meant in jest.

But it does make clear that this proof was a longstanding interest of Alpöge’s, and he had some insights into how to connect different areas of math to reach the final proof. The process seems to have involved getting the AI started with handling a simplified “toy” form of some of Alpöge’s insights and then directing it to expand what it found there to the full scope of the Riemann hypothesis.

The proof itself comes in two different forms, and the difference between them gets at the heart of why AI usage in math has been controversial. One is a rigorous description of the proof using a programming language named Lean that has allowed the rapid verification that the proof is valid. The second is a description of the logic behind it, which may ultimately be the key for mathematics as a field to benefit from this proof.

## Proof factories

It’s important to emphasize that, so far at least, AI has been solving problems that humans previously recognized as significant. That significance is typically ascribed to mathematical ideas because of their implications or utility—they either tell us something about areas of math that people care about, or they keep popping up in problems that mathematicians are working on. So far, there are no indications that AI can recognize or formulate interesting and important unresolved problems on its own.

But AI has tackled many problems humans have considered significant with impressive ease. Trained on a body of material that included a lot of advanced math, the software has provided both formal proofs as well as counterexamples that have clearly demonstrated that some proposals are incorrect.

When it comes to proofs, AI might have some advantages over people. For starters, it’s not specialized in specific fields of math and can potentially pull together tools from a variety of disciplines. AI also pays no cost (either in terms of career or emotional soundness) from going down the wrong track, giving up, and starting over.

AI models have also had one of their biggest limitations removed via humanity’s development of Lean, a computer language that allows mathematical proofs to be expressed in a way that can be readily verified. Due to their tendency to hallucinate, a description of a proof generated by an AI would still require extensive human validation before it could be accepted, a task that might radically shift the effort/reward ratio of using AI models. But by instructing an AI to include the necessary Lean code as part of its output, verification has become straightforward.

The unfortunate aspect of this for mathematics as a field is that it’s often the process of working through the reasoning behind a proof, rather than the step-by-step logic, that advances the field as a whole.

## Deriving worries

Mathematicians have expressed their fears about this aspect of AI usage in a formal open letter . We’ll try to connect those fears to the recent announcement.

Before AI, proofs were typically worked through by people who recognized potential pathways connecting disparate fields of math and spent years finding ways to formalize those intuitions and validate that the math worked. It wasn’t necessarily an efficient use of time if the only output was the proof itself.

But that was rarely the case. By finding the connections between problems, this work helped many other people see new ways of tackling whatever issues they were wrestling with. Mathematicians often developed new tools, found shortcuts, or stumbled across related problems while working through their proofs, enriching math as a whole. In other words, the proof itself was often less important for math than the process of generating it.

Indeed, nobody can say much about the Riemann proof at the moment, simply because mathematicians have barely started the process of shifting through the logic as expressed in Lean. It’s possible it can eventually produce new insights and tools, but it may take years before humans can figure out what they are and how to express them in a way that other mathematicians can appreciate.

How mathematicians are expected to identify new challenges that can push their fields beyond the current body while seeing AI relieve them of the need to actually do math is anybody’s guess.

This is all new and progressing incredibly quickly; there has been no time for the field to find a new normal. It’s possible that, once Alpöge gets around to describing the approach he pushed Claude to use, mathematicians will start getting the same sorts of insights that they normally expect to receive from proofs. It could be that Alpöge’s approach, mixing human intuition with machine-generated detail and rigor, provides a model for what math will look like in a few years.

But it’s impossible to tell at this early stage in development.

title: A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space
subtitle: Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stars spread heavy elements into space with their stellar winds.
feedText: This material eventually forms more stars, and even rocky planets like ours. For a long time, astronomers thought this important mass-loss was driven by stellar winds. But new research shows how magnetic fields play an important role. A vast flare and magnetic loop of material from the AGB star Mira provides the evidence.
articleBody:
# A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space

Highly-evolved stars spread the material for new planets and stars into space with their stellar winds. These stars are called aysmptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, and they're cool, luminous stars that are running out of hydrogen and leaving the main sequence behind. As they age, they can shed as much as 30 Earth masses of material per year into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The material is first emitted in pulses of gas, and eventually that gas cools into dust and the star's radiation pressure pushes it away with its stellar wind. Carbon and silica are important parts of what's emitted, and silica is the main building block for rocky planets, while carbon feeds into organic particles. So these stellar winds from AGB stars clearly play an important role in the formation of planets, other stars, and even potential life.

Researchers at Chalmers University in Sweden have been observing Mira, an AGB star about 300 light years away. It's the prototype and namesake of what are called Mira variables, pulsating AGB stars that are oxygen-rich. Their results are challenging the long-held understanding that stellar winds driven by radiation pressure are what spread heavy elements into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The research is " A giant magnetic eruption from the asymptotic-giant-branch star Mira A ," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. The lead author is Wouter Vlemmings, Professor in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg, Sweden.

"Mass loss during the advanced evolutionary stages of low- and intermediate-mass stars is traditionally attributed to dust-driven winds, whereas the influence of magnetic fields remains poorly constrained," the authors write. "This mass-loss process is crucial for the chemical enrichment of the Universe."

Since this type of mass-loss is so fundamental, it's attracted a lot of attention and is the subject of a huge amount of research. In this work, the researchers used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations to study how Mira's magnetic fields might shape its mass loss. ALMA can't directly observe magnetic fields; instead it observes them indirectly through their polarizing effect on radio emissions.

“For decades, astronomers have believed that the winds from stars like this must be powered by starlight. Light from the star shines on grains of dust in the star’s outer atmosphere, and that gives them a push. But this star is showing us something different: that strong magnetic fields can also shape and power stellar winds. That changes a fundamental part of the origin story of the atoms we ourselves are made of," lead author Vlemmings explained in a press release .

This schematic shows the structure of an AGB star, from its degenerate core to its circumstellar envelope. It shows it during its thermal pulse stage, when pulses drive gas outward, where it cools and forms dust in the envelope. Radiation pressure generates the stellar wind that drives the dust away into the ISM. Image Credit: Lu et al. Front. Astron. Space Sci., 23 July 2025. Sec. Astrostatistics

Astrophysicists have detected strong magnetic fields in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars like Mira, and researchers have suggested that they may play a role in driving their mass loss. But the researchers explain that there's been no empirical evidence of the role magnetic fields play in the process, and that wind-driven mass loss models don't include magnetic fields.

Recent observations, however, are challenging the overall understanding of the wind-driven mass loss scenario. Some AGB stars show mass-loss but also show insufficient dust to explain it. These stars are oxygen-rich AGB stars like Mira. Since Mira is the nearest of its type of dusty, pulsation-driven O-rich AGB stars, it makes sense to study it.

Both ALMA and the Very Large Array recently observed Mira A, the AGB star, and its companion Mira B, a white dwarf, in August 2025. But observations go back ten years, and both sets of data combine to reveal dramatic changes on Mira A's surface.

"During the past decade, high-angular-resolution observations of Mira A at visible, millimetre, and submillimetre wavelengths have revealed several unexpected phenomena related to the stellar atmosphere and mass-loss process," the authors write.

This ten-year study of Mira's surface is the longest study of any star other than the Sun.

This time-lapse shows ten years of changes on the surface of Mira A. Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

“We were astonished to see how the star’s surface is constantly changing. The brightest areas were different every time we looked, and the brightest patches are amazingly bright. We realised that star is flaring, releasing vast amounts of energy each time," said study co-author Miora Andriantsaralaza, a postdoctoral researcher in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology.

Some of the hotspots in the video have brightness temperatures of 8,000 Kelvin. That's far higher than the average 2,000 K brightness temperature.

But the main finding is what researchers call SiO (silicon monoxide) masers. They're often found in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars, just inside the dust formation zone. But Mira A's masers are at a much greater distance, where the gas is too thin for a strong SiO maser to form. So the researchers say the masers trace a shock moving outward, and that it has much higher density than expected. In short, a flare that expanded into a huge loop of expelled material.

“In 2023, we saw one of these flares appear on the star’s surface, but it didn’t stop there. Over the next two years, this eruption on the surface created a vast, expanding loop of gas around the star, which we captured in an image in 2025. The loop was much bigger than the star, extending as far out as the distance of Saturn from the Sun. We hadn’t seen anything like that before," said co-author Behzad Bojnordi Arbab, a doctoral student at Chalmers University.

Masers aren't always polarised, but these ones are linearly and circularly polarized. Linearly polarised means its polarisation is organized, and the polarising is shaping it. Circular means it rotates in a corkscrew pattern. Taken together, the astronomers used those features to map Mira's magnetic field geometry. That in turn let them understand how the magnetism is shaping its wind and its mass loss.

The loop and its polarisation is the key in this work.

“In the loop, there’s a strong magnetic field, which must also influence the star’s wind. That showed us a connection between the flare and the loop, and reminded us also of phenomena we can see on our Sun," said Vlemmings.

This figure from the research shows a three-dimensional representation of the adopted magnetic-loop ejection model anchored to the surface of Mira. The structure is colour coded according to line-of-sight velocity. Image Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

For now, the source of these magnetic fields isn't entirely clear. "The origin of the magnetic fields responsible for the observed ejections remains uncertain, although several mechanisms have been proposed," the authors write. A turbulent dynamo deep in Mira's convective envelope could be responsible, or differential rotation between the star's core and envelope could be behind them. Making progress understanding how the magnetic fields drive mass loss will depend on understanding how they're generated.

The flares and magnetic fields are evidence of a new element in mass-loss. On our Sun, flares are generated by magnetic fields, and they're associated with coronal mass ejections , where material is sent speeding away from the Sun. But our Sun is young, and isn't an aged AGB star experiencing the same level of mass loss. Still, these findings draw a parallel between the two.

“Now we see that magnetic storms on Mira’s surface are continually creating bright flares. Even more surprisingly, each of these is strong enough to lift parts of the star’s outer layers and launch them into interstellar space,” said Andriantsaralaza.

This research shows that our understanding of AGB mass-loss has to take into account magnetic fields, not just radiation-driven stellar winds.

"The discovery of coronal-mass-ejection-style eruptions from an AGB star redefines our understanding of late-stage stellar evolution," the authors write. They can help explain some of the features of AGB mass-loss, like clumpiness, asymmetry, and time variability. They can also help explain some of the morphologies of planetary nebulae , the beautiful shells of ionized gas ejected by aged stars.

"Consequently, magnetic activity must be integrated into models as a dynamically dominant force in initiating mass loss and shaping circumstellar environments," the authors conclude in their study. And since AGB mass loss spreads the stuff of planets into the ISM, that could explain, at least partly, why we're here.

“Our study has consequences for our understanding of the whole of the galaxy’s ecosystem. Perhaps, Earth wouldn’t be here if it wasn’t for magnetic storms on a red giant star, billions of years ago before the Sun was born," said Vlemmings.

### Evan Gough

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

articleBody:
Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water.

The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with [1,638 cases as of November 23](https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles). Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died.

## Deaths and transmission

On November 23, Pennsylvania's health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its [third measles death](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/news/releases/112426.htm), an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, [an infant](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/news/releases/110526.htm) and [a child](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/news/releases/111326.htm). New York has also reported a [death, which was of a 7-month-old baby](https://publications.aap.org/aapnews/news/36693/AAP-president-Child-s-death-in-New-York-another?autologincheck=redirected). On November 20, Virginia reported the death of [a child between the age of 0 and 4](https://www.vdh.virginia.gov/news/public-relations-contacts/2026-news-releases/vdh-1st-measles-death-2026/).

articleBody:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to staff during his first all-hands since returning to the company, while attempting to distance himself from the narrative that the White House and tech leaders helped him get his job back, according to [reports from Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-24/nvidia-s-huang-to-host-all-hands-meeting-a-day-after-his-return) *,* [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/24/technology/jensen-huang-apology-nvidia-ceo.html), and [The Handbasket's Marisa Kabas](https://bsky.app/profile/marisakabas.bsky.social/post/3n33bk6pymk2s).

During the meeting, Huang reportedly called claims that President Donald Trump was directly involved in his reinstatement - an idea [publicly promoted by Trump himself](https://www.theverge.com/policy/1040096/trump-nvidia-jensen-huang-reinstated) - "completely untrue." He added, "Don't think for a second politics played a role in the company. We are the most apolitical company," [according to Kabas](https://bsky.app/profile/marisakabas.bsky.social/post/3n33bk6pymk2s).

title: Does It Really Matter If There’s an Intelligence Explosion?
subtitle:

articleBody:
Noah Smith at *Noahpinion*:

“Pacing the frontier” so that alignment research can catch up might be effective in a world of steady linear AI progress. But in a world of sudden superexponential progress, AI alignment research will immediately be left behind. Even if there is a Singularity for understanding alignment, in a world with an intelligence explosion it will be the superintelligent AI, not us, that carries out that Singularity and decides on its alignment for itself.

A second point is that it’s not obvious why an intelligence explosion would be more dangerous than — or even distinguishable from — the type of rapid, non-explosive progress we’re already getting. Remember, AI going from “can’t add two numbers together” to “solves problems too hard for all human mathematicians combined” in three years is *not* counted as an intelligence explosion!

It’s clear that at the current rate of steady progress, AI will become superhuman in most domains in a fairly small number of years. Even robotics and other physical tasks [look conquerable](https://www.understandingrobots.org/p/openais-astra-model-is-shockingly) with the current type of AI that powers Claude and GPT. This means that AI will basically look like a god within our lifetimes, *whether or not* it looks like the kind of infinitely self-improving gods that populate Vernor Vinge novels.

This is why I’m not sure what an intelligence explosion means for our economy. It’s [easy to write down a model](https://aleximas.substack.com/p/will-ai-soon-lead-to-double-digit) in which smoothly increasing AI capabilities drive a smooth increase in GDP. But why should we believe a model like that?

More [↗ noahpinion.blog](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/does-it-really-matter-if-theres-an).

# Skipper, Tripod, and finding apps that fit

- Skipper, Tripod, and finding apps that fit – Six Colors MENU This Week's Sponsor Magic Lasso Adblock : Block ads in iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple TV apps By Jason Snell November 24, 2026 12:00 PM PT ■ apps Skipper, Tripod, and finding apps that fit We live in a world with so many monolithic apps and services, dominated by giant companies. So one of my favorite things is to explore little software niches that haven’t been captured by the major players. Instead of one or two pretty samey apps, you can end up with a whole forest of wild variations on the theme, each fueled by developers making specific choices about how to present information and serve users. When I compare these apps, I realize that there’s really no right or wrong—there are just choices, some of which might work for me, some of which won’t. I’m not offended when an app isn’t made for me, but I can be delighted when an app does slide perfectly into my life. After a year of using Television Time (not to be confused with the now-defunct TV Time ) to log my TV viewing and (more importantly) let me keep track of what we’re watching next and what we’d like to get to next, I discovered an app that just served me better. That’s Skipper , Yoav Zoldan’s new app, available for $30/year or $3/month. What sold me on it is that its primary screen is a list of shows I’m watching with the next episode marked, sorted in a way that makes sense to me. I only want to interact with the app in a handful of ways: seeing what to watch next, checking the box indicating that we watched it, and occasionally searching to add a show that I might be interested in watching next. Television Time required more swiping around and entering detail views, and one thing I’ve discovered about myself is that I prefer apps that are optimized to present all the information I want in one place, and which limit the number of swipes and taps required to navigate around. Skipper hit that sweet spot for me—your mileage, of course, may vary. Skipper has a lot of other features, including a very clever one that compares your watch list to your streaming service subscriptions and can nudge you to drop that service you’re not actually using, complete with a calendar of when shows you watch will be returning. (I know, I know, I shouldn’t have subscribed to BritBox. I have no time to watch it!) It’s not entirely accurate—it doesn’t seem to understand that I watch sports on YouTube TV and things that are not shows on YouTube Premium—but it’s a smart feature that could help a lot of people who are not inveterate streaming subscription sickos like me. Just as there are many TV-tracking apps, there are many, many podcast apps. I’ve been using Overcast for ages , and it just fits into how I want to listen to podcasts. I spend as little time as possible picking what to listen to (there’s my optimization streak again) and have Overcast configured to give me that. But there have been other podcast apps that serve other, equally valid, points of view. Castro really made its name by not just offering a beautiful interface, but a clever “triage” system that brings new episodes into an inbox. Then the user manually decides what’s worth adding to the play queue. Clearly that approach clicked with a lot of people, making Castro a fan favorite even through its ongoing business challenges and different owners . Which brings me to an impressive new podcast app that’s been designed to appeal especially to Castro fans: Ben Rice McCarthy’s Tripod . Ben is a really talented designer, and the app looks gorgeous and works well. It’s built around the same Inbox concept as Castro, so Castro users will feel right at home. I got to beta test Ben’s app for a while, and was incredibly impressed—especially at how it works on the iPhone Duo. That all said, I am just not the target audience for Tripod—and that’s okay. The way Overcast works for podcasts is the way I want to work. Quite frankly, the idea of having another Inbox to check does not fill my heart with joy, even if the podcasts found therein would bring me that joy. That’s on me, not on Ben, and not on Tripod. So if you watch TV like me, you should try Skipper . And if you’re not like me, you should try Tripod . That’s the beauty of these app niches; they don’t have to be all things to all people, they just need to find their audience and serve them well. Report a typo

articleBody:
Explore This Section

- [Science](https://science.nasa.gov/)
- [Citizen Science](https://science.nasa.gov/citizen-science/)
- Amateur Astronomer? Be a…
- [Overview](https://science.nasa.gov/learn)
- [Resources](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/resources)
- [Opportunities](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/learner-opportunities/)
- [Citizen Science](https://science.nasa.gov/citizen-science/)
- [Highlights](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/science-activation-highlights)
- [About Science Activation](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/about-science-activation/)

Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a [kilonova](https://science.nasa.gov/universe/glossary/#kilonova). These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory can watch the whole sky. But if you have a telescope with a camera, or access to one, you can help find and follow these cosmic fireworks as a part of NASA’s [Kilonova Catcher](https://science.nasa.gov/citizen-science/kilonova-catcher/?utm_medium=nasa-science&utm_source=summary-page&utm_campaign=launch-highlight) project!

Kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network. When [gravitational wave](https://science.nasa.gov/universe/glossary/#gravitational-waves) detectors or space telescopes send out an alert, volunteers point their own telescopes at the sky to help find and track the fading light. The network also follows up on gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the universe, and catches other short-lived cosmic events whenever the opportunity arises.

The Kilonova Catcher network has more than 150 registered members on several continents. Volunteers work side by side with professional astronomers and observatories. They have already contributed to more than 64 official reports shared through NASA’s General Coordinates Network, the system scientists use to share discoveries in real time. Volunteers’ observations have been credited for their contributions by being named authors in peer-reviewed scientific research papers. Kilonova Catcher volunteers also joined NASA’s lunar [Impact Flash!](https://science.nasa.gov/citizen-science/impact-flash/) project campaign during the Artemis II mission, recording the tiny flashes of light made when meteoroids strike the Moon. The network is getting ready to help follow up thousands of new alerts from NASA’s new [Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/).

“Here at Kilonova Catcher, by chasing the light from gravitational-wave events, we’re seeing how a single collision reaches across the universe,” said Cristina Andrade, Kilonova Catcher head of operations at the Minnesota Institute for Astrophysics. “The observatories that make this possible will produce an unprecedented amount of data. We need more human minds, more people with their eyes on the sky and on the data, both literally and figuratively. And more importantly, we need more people to realize they are capable of great feats of science, regardless of their background.”

The Kilonova Catcher project is co-led by Andrade and Principal Investigator Dr. Damien Turpin, a researcher at the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA). Damien said, “I am inspired by the expertise and drive of our amateur astronomers. They are always digging for more information and pushing the limits of their understanding. This science could not be done without their contributions.”

To register and become a Kilonova Catcher, visit [https://kilonovacatcher.in2p3.fr/](https://kilonovacatcher.in2p3.fr/) or send an email to kilonovacatcher@gmail.com. Anyone who has access to a telescope with a camera can take part!

On Aug. 17, 2017, the[Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory](https://www.ligo.caltech.edu/) (LIGO) and the[Virgo Interferometer](https://www.ego-gw.it/public/about/whatIs.aspx) both detected gravitational waves from the collision between two neutron stars. Within 12 hours observatories had identified the source of the event within the lenticular galaxy NGC 4993, shown in this image, which was gathered with NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope. The associated kilonova is clearly visible in the Hubble observations. This is the first time the optical counterpart of a gravitational wave event was observed. Hubble observed the kilonova gradually fading over the course of six days, as illustrated by the three time-stamped inset images made between Aug. 22 and 28.

## Learn More and Get Involved

## Kilonova Catcher

Use your backyard telescope to spot the most cataclysmic collisions in our Universe!
